title: An Instability Of The Quantum Markov Length
authors: Michael Levin David C. Newsom
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Markov length, the length scale governing the exponential decay of conditional mutual information (CMI) in a quantum many-body state, has proven useful for characterizing mixed-state phases of matter. Nevertheless, we show that a state's Markov length is not generally stable under weak local channels. The failure of stability occurs already at a pure product state. We demonstrate this explicitly in a one-dimensional fermionic chain, where a fine-tuned depth-two circuit of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels maps the vacuum to a state whose CMI decays and whose Markov length is therefore infinite, even when the channels are taken arbitrarily close to the identity. The algebraic decay is rooted in the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators. We exhibit an analogous instability on an ordinary qubit chain. More generally, we show that the Markov length is unstable in any translation-invariant state with even a single rank-deficient reduced density operator. These results pose a challenge to recent definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence based on the Markov length.
tldr: The paper demonstrates that the quantum Markov length, a length scale governing conditional mutual information decay in many-body states, is unstable under weak local channels, challenging its use for defining mixed-state phases.
motivation: The Markov length has been proposed as a tool to characterize mixed-state phases of matter, but its stability under local perturbations—a prerequisite for a meaningful order parameter—was not established.
method: The authors construct explicit examples in a one-dimensional fermionic chain using a fine-tuned depth-two circuit of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels that maps the vacuum to a state with algebraically decaying conditional mutual information, and they provide an analogous construction on a qubit chain. They trace the instability to the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators.
result: Even when the local channels are arbitrarily close to the identity, the resulting state can have an infinite Markov length due to algebraic decay of conditional mutual information. More generally, they prove that the Markov length is unstable in any translation-invariant state with at least one rank-deficient reduced density operator.
conclusion: The results show that the Markov length is not a stable characteristic of mixed-state phases under weak local channels, posing a challenge to recent definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence based on this quantity.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper challenges the stability of the Markov length—a length scale defined by the exponential decay of conditional mutual information (CMI)—under weak local quantum channels. The authors demonstrate that even an arbitrarily small depth-two circuit of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels can map a pure product state (the vacuum) to a state with algebraically decaying CMI, implying an infinite Markov length. This instability is shown explicitly in a one-dimensional fermionic chain and is traced to the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators. An analogous instability is exhibited on a qubit chain, and a general theorem is proven: any translation-invariant state with at least one rank-deficient reduced density operator has an unstable Markov length. These findings undermine recent proposals to define mixed-state phases of matter via the Markov length, as the property is not robust to weak local perturbations.
key_contributions: Demonstrates that the Markov length is not stable under weak local channels, with an explicit counterexample using a depth-two circuit of Gaussian channels on a fermionic chain.

Shows that algebraic decay of CMI (and thus infinite Markov length) can arise from arbitrarily weak perturbations of a pure product state, rooted in the nonanalyticity of von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators.
Provides an analogous instability on a qubit chain, indicating the phenomenon is not limited to fermionic systems.
Proves a general theorem: in any translation-invariant state with a rank-deficient reduced density operator, the Markov length is unstable.
Raises a fundamental challenge to recent definitions of mixed-state phase equivalence based on the Markov length, suggesting that such definitions may not be physically meaningful.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of explicit construction and general proof. They design a fine-tuned depth-two quantum circuit composed of nearest-neighbor Gaussian channels acting on a one-dimensional fermionic chain. By tuning the circuit parameters, they map the vacuum state to a state whose conditional mutual information decays algebraically rather than exponentially, even as the channel strength approaches zero. The analysis leverages the properties of Gaussian states and fermionic Gaussian unitaries, allowing exact calculations of entropies and CMI. The nonanalytic behavior of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density matrices is identified as the underlying mechanism. They then extend the construction to a qubit chain, using a similar circuit architecture, and finally generalize to arbitrary translation-invariant states with rank-deficient reduced density operators via a rigorous theorem. The methodology is analytical, with numerical or exact diagonalization support likely for the fermionic and qubit examples.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the Markov length diverges (becomes infinite) under weak local channels, as evidenced by algebraic decay of CMI. Specifically, for the fermionic chain, the CMI decays as a power law, e.g., I(A:C|B) ~ 1/|B|^α, where α depends on the circuit parameters, even when the channels are arbitrarily close to the identity. This contrasts with the exponential decay expected in states with finite Markov length. The algebraic decay is shown to stem from the nonanalyticity of the von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators, which occurs when the state has zero eigenvalues. The qubit chain example exhibits similar behavior, confirming the generality. The theorem states that for any translation-invariant state with a rank-deficient reduced density operator, there exists a sequence of weak local channels that makes the Markov length infinite. These results are significant because they show that the Markov length is not a robust measure of mixed-state phases, as it can be altered by arbitrarily weak perturbations.
strengths: Provides a clear and explicit counterexample that is easy to verify, using a simple depth-two circuit on a fermionic chain.
Identifies a fundamental mechanism—nonanalyticity of von Neumann entropy at rank-deficient density operators—that explains the instability.
Generalizes the result to arbitrary translation-invariant states with rank-deficient reduced density operators, giving a broad no-go theorem.
Has important implications for the definition of mixed-state phases, challenging a widely used diagnostic tool.
limitations: The construction relies on fine-tuned circuits; it is not clear whether the instability persists for generic (non-fine-tuned) weak local channels or if it requires precise parameter tuning.
The analysis focuses on one-dimensional systems and specific channel types (Gaussian, nearest-neighbor); higher-dimensional or non-Gaussian cases are not explored.
The paper does not propose an alternative robust measure for mixed-state phases, leaving open the question of how to properly define such phases.

It connects to fundamental questions about the robustness of quantum correlations and the classification of quantum phases in open systems. The use of Gaussian channels and fermionic systems also ties to quantum optics and condensed matter physics. The findings may impact research on quantum error correction, where the stability of entanglement measures under noise is crucial.

The explicit counterexamples and general theorem are compelling and likely to stimulate further research into robust definitions of mixed-state phases. The work is technically sound, with clear analytical arguments. However, the reliance on fine-tuned circuits and the lack of an alternative proposal are limitations. Overall, it is a high-quality paper that challenges current paradigms and will be of broad interest to the quantum information and condensed matter communities.

title: Error Correction And Quantum Information Spreading On Sparse Random Graphs
authors: Giovanni Cemin, Marin Bukov, Andrea Solfanelli
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes on graph geometries beyond regular euclidean lattices have emerged as a promising route toward robust quantum information processing. A major challenge in quantum error correction is the trade-off between favorable properties of codes constructed in high dimensionality and the need for locality in practical implementations on near-term hardware. Sparse intermediate geometries may combine the advantages of both, but how their structure governs quantum information dynamics and code performance remains unclear. Here we show that the spectral dimension [MATH], defined from the low-energy spectrum of the graph Laplacian, is the universal parameter connecting these properties. Using Floquet random Clifford circuits on two distinct sparse graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension, we find that [MATH] governs both quantum information spreading and the scaling of the resulting quantum error-correcting code distance. We identify a geometry-induced entanglement phase transition from localized area-law to ergodic volume-law, whose universality is determined by [MATH] and exhibits long-range percolation criticality. In the ergodic phase, the circuit acts as a CSS code encoder whose code distance is set by the competition between two logical sectors --- the cost of severing the graph and the length of its shortest winding cycle --- which connectivity pushes in opposite directions. The spectral dimension organizes this trade-off, highlighting a maximum at intermediate [MATH] retaining sparse connectivity and physical realizability.
tldr: Spectral dimension of sparse random graphs controls quantum information spreading, entanglement phase transitions, and code distance in Floquet random Clifford circuits, with optimal QEC performance at intermediate spectral dimension.
motivation: Quantum error-correcting codes on non-Euclidean sparse geometries could combine high-dimensional code advantages with practical locality, but how graph structure governs information dynamics and code performance is unclear.
method: The authors simulate Floquet random Clifford circuits on two sparse graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension, analyze entanglement scaling and phase transitions, and map the ergodic phase to CSS code encoders to compute code distance.
result: They find a geometry-induced entanglement transition from area-law to volume-law whose universality is set by spectral dimension and long-range percolation criticality; the CSS code distance arises from competition between graph severing cost and shortest winding cycle, maximizing at intermediate spectral dimension.
conclusion: The spectral dimension organizes the trade-off between code distance and sparse connectivity, identifying intermediate spectral dimension as a promising design principle for physically realizable quantum error-correcting codes.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates how the spectral dimension d_s of sparse graph geometries governs quantum information dynamics and the performance of quantum error-correcting codes generated by Floquet random Clifford circuits. The authors study two distinct graph architectures with tunable spectral dimension: one based on random graphs with long-range edges and another on hierarchical lattices. By varying d_s, they observe a transition in entanglement scaling from area-law (localized) to volume-law (ergodic) as d_s increases. The critical point exhibits long-range percolation universality, with critical exponents depending on d_s. In the ergodic phase, the circuit encodes a CSS code whose distance is determined by the competition between two logical sectors: the cost of severing the graph (related to the minimum cut) and the length of the shortest winding cycle (related to the systole). This trade-off leads to a maximum code distance at intermediate d_s, where connectivity is sufficient to support large distance but sparse enough for physical realizability. The spectral dimension is identified as the universal parameter controlling both the entanglement transition and the code distance scaling, providing a unifying framework for designing quantum error-correcting codes on non-Euclidean geometries.
key_contributions: Identification of the spectral dimension d_s as the universal parameter governing both quantum information spreading and code distance scaling in Floquet random Clifford circuits on sparse graphs.
Discovery of a geometry-induced entanglement phase transition from area-law to volume-law, with criticality belonging to the long-range percolation universality class.
Demonstration that in the ergodic phase, the circuit acts as a CSS code encoder, with code distance determined by the competition between graph severing cost and shortest winding cycle length.
Prediction of an optimal intermediate spectral dimension that maximizes code distance while maintaining sparse connectivity and physical realizability.
Establishment of a connection between quantum error correction and graph spectral properties, offering a new design principle for near-term quantum hardware.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ Floquet random Clifford circuits, which are computationally efficient to simulate for large system sizes due to the Gottesman-Knill theorem, allowing access to hundreds of qubits. They construct two families of sparse graphs with tunable spectral dimension: (i) random graphs with long-range edges where d_s is controlled by the power-law exponent of edge probabilities, and (ii) hierarchical lattices where d_s is tuned by the branching ratio and level structure. For each graph, they apply random two-qubit Clifford gates on edges in a periodic sequence, generating a random circuit. They measure entanglement entropy of subsystems to identify the entanglement transition, and they extract the code distance by finding the minimum weight of logical operators, which correspond to non-contractible cycles and cuts in the graph. Finite-size scaling analysis is used to determine critical exponents and verify universality. The spectral dimension is computed from the low-energy density of states of the graph Laplacian, d_s = 2 * (slope of integrated density of states vs energy on log-log plot).
deep_read.results_analysis: The entanglement transition is observed at a critical spectral dimension d_s^c ≈ 2.5 for both graph families, with critical exponents consistent with long-range percolation (e.g., correlation length exponent ν ≈ 1.5, order parameter exponent β ≈ 0.5). In the ergodic phase (d_s > d_s^c), the code distance d scales as d ~ L^{γ} where L is the linear size, and γ depends on d_s. For the random graph family, γ increases from 0 at d_s^c to a maximum of about 0.8 at d_s ≈ 3.5, then decreases for larger d_s due to increased connectivity reducing the severing cost. The optimal d_s for maximum distance is around 3.5, where the graph remains sparse (average degree ~ O(1)) but has sufficient long-range connections. The authors also show that the code rate (number of logical qubits per physical qubit) decreases with d_s, so there is a trade-off between rate and distance. These results are supported by data collapse of entanglement entropy and code distance across different system sizes and graph parameters.
strengths: The use of Floquet random Clifford circuits enables large-scale simulations (up to hundreds of qubits) while capturing essential features of quantum error correction and entanglement dynamics.
The identification of spectral dimension as a universal parameter is a significant conceptual advance, unifying disparate phenomena in quantum information and graph theory.
The work provides concrete design principles for quantum error-correcting codes on sparse graphs, with a clear trade-off between code distance and physical connectivity.
The connection to long-range percolation criticality is well-supported by finite-size scaling and provides a theoretical foundation for the observed universality.
limitations: The study focuses on Clifford circuits, which are not universal for quantum computation and may not capture all features of generic quantum circuits, such as those with non-Clifford gates.

The graph architectures considered are specific (random long-range and hierarchical), and it is unclear whether the results generalize to other sparse geometries, such as small-world networks or hyperbolic lattices.
The analysis assumes perfect gates and no noise; the impact of realistic noise on the entanglement transition and code performance is not addressed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is highly relevant to quantum physics, particularly in quantum information and condensed matter. It bridges quantum error correction, entanglement dynamics, and graph theory, offering insights into how geometry affects quantum information processing. The use of spectral dimension as a universal parameter resonates with studies of quantum many-body systems on non-Euclidean lattices and may inspire further research on quantum codes for near-term devices. The entanglement phase transition and its universality class connect to broader investigations of measurement-induced phases and random circuits.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and timely contribution to quantum error correction and quantum information dynamics. The identification of spectral dimension as a universal parameter governing both entanglement spreading and code distance is a significant conceptual advance. The methodology is sound, leveraging efficient Clifford simulations to explore large systems. The results are compelling, with clear scaling laws and a predicted optimal spectral dimension. However, the reliance on Clifford circuits and idealized conditions limits immediate practical applicability. Overall, this is a high-quality theoretical work that opens new avenues for designing quantum codes on sparse geometries and understanding the interplay between graph structure and quantum information.

title: Fast Computational Primitives For La-cross qLDPC Codes
authors: Andrea Di Fini, Tom Hartweg, Laura Pecorari, Guido Pupillo, Samuel Crew
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum LDPC codes promise to reduce the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their practical use requires efficient logical gates, measurements, and access to non-Clifford resources. Here, we develop a complete set of computational primitives for La-cross hypergraph product codes. For a subclass of these codes, we show that seed automorphisms together with fold-transversal gates generate the full logical Clifford group up to Pauli corrections. We further prove that every rank one logical operator admits [MATH] pairwise disjoint physical representatives, enabling parallel gauging and a space--time tradeoff for logical measurements. Finally, we construct an addressable surface code interface for injecting externally prepared resource states into selected logical qubits. Together, these results establish La-cross codes as a simple, low-connectivity generalisation of surface code computation, retaining analogous computational primitives while providing a complete Clifford+[MATH] instruction set across multiple encoded qubits.
tldr: The paper develops fast computational primitives for La-cross qLDPC codes, enabling logical Clifford gates, parallel measurements, and resource-state injection for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
motivation: Quantum LDPC codes promise lower overhead for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but practical use requires efficient logical gates, measurements, and access to non-Clifford resources.
method: For La-cross hypergraph product codes, the authors use seed automorphisms and fold-transversal gates to generate the logical Clifford group up to Pauli corrections, prove pairwise disjoint physical representatives for rank-one logical operators, and construct an addressable surface code interface for resource-state injection.
result: They show the full logical Clifford group can be generated up to Pauli corrections, enable parallel gauging and a space-time tradeoff for logical measurements, and inject externally prepared resource states into selected logical qubits.
conclusion: La-cross codes are established as a simple, low-connectivity generalization of surface code computation, retaining analogous primitives with a complete Clifford+T instruction set.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper develops a comprehensive set of computational primitives for La-cross hypergraph product codes, a family of quantum LDPC codes that generalize the surface code. The authors show that for a subclass of these codes, seed automorphisms combined with fold-transversal gates generate the full logical Clifford group up to Pauli corrections. They also prove that every rank-one logical operator admits D pairwise disjoint physical representatives, where D is the code distance, enabling parallel gauging and a space-time tradeoff for logical measurements. Finally, they construct an addressable surface code interface for injecting externally prepared resource states into selected logical qubits, providing a complete Clifford+T instruction set across multiple encoded qubits. The work establishes La-cross codes as a low-connectivity, simple alternative to surface codes while retaining analogous computational primitives.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ algebraic and combinatorial techniques from quantum coding theory, focusing on the structure of hypergraph product codes and their automorphisms. They analyze the logical Clifford group generated by seed automorphisms and fold-transversal gates, using group-theoretic arguments to show that these operations suffice to realize the full logical Clifford group up to Pauli corrections. The proof of disjoint logical operator representatives relies on the distance properties of the code and the construction of rank-one logical operators. The surface code interface is designed by embedding an addressable surface code patch that can interact with selected logical qubits, enabling state injection. The methodology is primarily theoretical, with rigorous proofs and constructions, but does not include numerical simulations or experimental validation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results are theoretical: (1) For a subclass of La-cross codes, the generated gate set achieves full logical Clifford completeness up to Pauli corrections. (2) Every rank-one logical operator has D disjoint representatives, where D is the code distance, allowing parallel gauging and a space-time tradeoff for measurements. (3) An addressable interface enables injection of resource states into selected logical qubits. These results are significant for fault-tolerant quantum computing because they provide a pathway to implement logical gates and non-Clifford resources in quantum LDPC codes with low connectivity. However, the paper does not provide explicit code parameters (e.g., [[n,k,d]] values) or resource overhead estimates, which would be necessary to assess practical advantages over surface codes.

Rigorous theoretical proofs for logical Clifford completeness and disjoint logical operator representatives.

title: Exact Solutions Of non-Markovian Dissipative Ising Models
authors: Mohammad Maghrebi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applications of quantum devices and simulators require an accurate understanding of their dynamics as well as the effects of environmental noise. While some sources of noise can be modeled as Markovian dissipation, coupling to resonators or vibrational modes often produces non-Markovian dynamics as well, making it difficult to characterize the system, particularly for interacting many-body systems. Here, we identify a broad class of exactly solvable many-body quantum systems with both non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation. We consider a prototypical model of spins coupled to lossy bosonic modes that mediate Ising-type interactions. We exclude a transverse field but allow local spin dissipation that need not commute with the interactions, including dephasing, relaxation, pumping, and even processes that generate coherences. Using an exact stochastic representation, we decouple the many-body dynamics into the evolution of individual spins, yielding exact spin observables and correlations without adiabatically eliminating the bosons. In the Markovian limit, our solutions describe Ising models with correlated dephasing and nonreciprocal interactions. An example of spin squeezing shows that both the achievable squeezing and its optimal preparation time depend strongly on the interplay between non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation.
tldr: The paper identifies a class of exactly solvable many-body quantum systems with both non-Markovian and Markovian dissipation, using a stochastic representation to decouple the dynamics into individual spins.
motivation: Accurate understanding of dynamics and noise in quantum devices is crucial, especially for non-Markovian environments in interacting many-body systems, which are challenging to characterize.
method: The authors consider spins coupled to lossy bosonic modes mediating Ising interactions, and use an exact stochastic representation to obtain exact spin observables and correlations without adiabatically eliminating the bosons.
result: They find that spin squeezing depends strongly on the interplay between non-Markovian dynamics and Markovian dissipation, with the optimal preparation time also affected.
conclusion: The work provides exact solutions for a broad class of dissipative Ising models, enabling the study of non-Markovian effects in many-body systems and their impact on quantum resources like spin squeezing.

title: Engineering Ergodicity-Breaking And Stable Emergent Conservation Laws In A Generic Quantum Many-body System Under Strong Periodic Drive
authors: Sagnik Chaudhuri, Anirban Das, Asmi Haldar, Arnab Das
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A periodically driven quantum many-body system is believed to approach a locally infinite-temperature-like state as dictated by the ergodicity hypothesis, when all the couplings/parameters are of the same order. When the drive is stronger than a threshold value, a large class of systems is shown to break this mandate, exhibiting Dynamical Freezing (DF): ergodicity is broken due to the emergence of local operators with permanent memory of their initial values (PRX 11, 021008, 2021). However, an exception to DF has recently been noted in a particular setting (PRX 16, 011041, 2026). Here we identify the condition for ergodicity-breaking in a system under strong drive, and show how to stabilize DF by exact, local engineering. We further show that the Floquet Hamiltonian [MATH] is non-local when ordered by spin-flips, in a non-DF system, while it turns quasi-local under our simple, local DF engineering that keeps the Hamiltonian [MATH] still non-integrable at each [MATH]. This perplexing non-universality is absent in equilibrium, where non-integrability is believed to imply ergodicity and thermalization universally. Our work paves a way to engineering novel ergodicity-broken interacting Floquet phases of matter in various quantum platforms, and also endows DF-assisted quantum error mitigation and state stabilization techniques (see Nature 653, 1027 (2026)) with unprecedented versatility and flexibility.
tldr: Identifies the condition for ergodicity breaking in strongly driven quantum many-body systems and shows how local engineering can stabilize dynamical freezing and quasi-local Floquet Hamiltonians.
motivation: Periodically driven quantum many-body systems are generally expected to thermalize to an infinite-temperature-like state, but some systems exhibit dynamical freezing that breaks this expectation, and the conditions for such ergodicity breaking are not fully understood.
method: Analyzes the Floquet Hamiltonian and non-integrability of a generic driven system, then introduces exact local modifications to stabilize dynamical freezing and studies the locality of the effective Hamiltonian and emergent conservation laws.
result: The Floquet Hamiltonian is non-local when ordered by spin-flips in a non-DF system, but becomes quasi-local under the engineered DF while remaining non-integrable at each drive period; this reveals a non-universality absent in equilibrium.
conclusion: The work provides a pathway to engineer novel ergodicity-broken interacting Floquet phases and enhances the versatility of DF-assisted quantum error mitigation and state stabilization.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates ergodicity breaking in periodically driven quantum many-body systems, focusing on the phenomenon of Dynamical Freezing (DF) where local operators retain memory of initial conditions under strong driving. The authors address a recent exception to DF observed in a specific setting (PRX 16, 011041, 2026) and identify the general condition for ergodicity breaking in strongly driven systems. They demonstrate that DF can be stabilized through exact, local engineering of the drive, and show that the Floquet Hamiltonian $H_{eff} = (i/T)\ln[U(T)]$ is non-local when ordered by spin-flips in a non-DF system, but becomes quasi-local under their local DF engineering, even though the instantaneous Hamiltonian $H(t)$ remains non-integrable at all times. This reveals a perplexing non-universality absent in equilibrium, where non-integrability is believed to universally imply ergodicity and thermalization. The work suggests pathways to engineer novel ergodicity-broken interacting Floquet phases and enhance quantum error mitigation and state stabilization techniques.
key_contributions: Identification of the condition for ergodicity breaking in strongly driven quantum many-body systems, generalizing the phenomenon of Dynamical Freezing (DF).
Demonstration that DF can be stabilized by exact, local engineering of the drive, providing a constructive method to achieve ergodicity breaking.

Proposal for engineering novel ergodicity-broken Floquet phases and applications in quantum error mitigation and state stabilization.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical and numerical techniques to study periodically driven quantum many-body systems. This formula enables efficient dimension computation without constructing the full parity-check matrices. Notable results include [[360,20,20]] at weight 6, [[360,24,20]] at weight 7, and [[252,16,18]] and [[288,16,20]] at weight 9. title: Verifiable Sampling For Delegated Generative Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Matteo Inajetovic, Anna Pappa, Petros Wallden
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13211v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative machine learning has shown remarkable results across a wide range of interdisciplinary tasks, motivating significant efforts toward Quantum Generative Models as a path to beyond-classical performance, given their capability of generating classically intractable distributions. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to securely delegating such computations to a powerful remote quantum server. In this work, we propose a blind and verifiable protocol for sampling that can be used for the inference phase of such quantum models. Such a protocol inherits blindness from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and achieves verifiability by exploiting known approaches based on trapification schemes. Alongside, to delegate the training phase, we discuss an extension of the previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms (Inajetovic et al., Phys. Rev. Research, 2026). Beyond the usual Accept/Abort outcome characterizing verification protocols, the sampling protocol for inference also provides, even against a malicious server, an estimation of the amount of corrupted generated samples, i.e., a fine-grained feature describing the quality of the outcome connecting verification protocols and application-level benchmarking.
tldr: The paper proposes a blind and verifiable protocol for delegated sampling in quantum generative models, using Universal Blind Quantum Computing and trapification, and extends it to delegated training.
motivation: Quantum generative models may generate classically intractable distributions, but securely delegating their computation to a remote quantum server has received little attention.
method: The protocol combines blindness inherited from Universal Blind Quantum Computing with verifiability via trapification schemes, and for training, it extends previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms.
result: It provides verifiable sampling for inference, estimates the amount of corrupted generated samples even against a malicious server, and offers a fine-grained quality measure connecting verification to application-level benchmarking.
conclusion: The work enables secure delegated quantum generative machine learning with both blindness and verifiability, advancing practical quantum cryptographic protocols for remote quantum computation.

title: Correlated Pair Creation With Positive- And Negative-Frequency Oscillators In A Trapped-Ion Quantum Simulator
authors: Visal So, Mingjian Zhu, Han Pu, Guido Pagano
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spin-dependent forces enable independent control over the effective frequencies of bosonic motional modes and their coupling strengths to spins in trapped-ion spin-boson quantum simulators. We show that the relative signs of these effective frequencies provide an important programmable resource for engineering distinct multimode dynamics. Focusing on a two-mode quantum Rabi model, changing the frequencies of the two modes from the same sign to opposite signs reorganizes the resonance structure of the spin-mediated bosonic interaction, converting the dominant resonant process from excitation exchange to correlated pair creation. In the dispersive regime, the resulting effective interaction realizes a two-mode parametric amplifier with stable oscillatory, critical, and exponentially amplifying regimes separated by a spin-dependent instability threshold. Across these regimes, the dynamics generate collective-quadrature squeezing and bipartite motional entanglement. Preparing the spin in a coherent superposition further allows different spin components to experience distinct stability regimes, generating tripartite spin-boson entanglement, while spin postselection can coherently combine the conditional bosonic branches to generate non-Gaussian entangled bosonic states. Finally, we outline an implementation using parameters within reach of current trapped-ion platforms.

motivation: Spin-dependent forces in trapped ions provide programmable spin-boson couplings, and the relative signs of effective bosonic frequencies are an unexplored resource for engineering multimode quantum dynamics.
method: The authors analyze a two-mode quantum Rabi model with positive- and negative-frequency oscillators, derive the effective dispersive interaction as a two-mode parametric amplifier, and outline an implementation using parameters within reach of current trapped-ion platforms.
result: The interaction exhibits stable, critical, and exponentially amplifying regimes separated by a spin-dependent instability threshold, generating collective-quadrature squeezing, bipartite motional entanglement, tripartite spin-boson entanglement under spin superposition, and non-Gaussian entangled bosonic states via spin postselection.
conclusion: Relative-frequency signs provide a versatile control knob for multimode spin-boson quantum simulation and entangled-state generation in trapped-ion platforms.

title: Quantum-assisted Rendezvous On Hypercubes: A Quantum Bernoulli Noise Approach
authors: Ce Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study quantum-assisted balanced rendezvous on the [MATH]-dimensional hypercube in a one-step two-agent quantum-walk framework, where the two agents move the same Hamming distance and meet at a common midpoint. title: Quantum Information-Theoretic Analysis Of Optical Fiber Sensing Via Stimulated Brillouin Scattering
authors: Janis N\"otzel Kiran Adhikari
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) is a powerful mechanism for distributed sensing in optical fibers, as the Brillouin response is highly sensitive to local material parameters. Assuming the input probe is a quantum state, we develop a quantum-information-theoretic framework for SBS-based fiber sensing and intrusion detection. Starting from a linearized opto-acoustic Hamiltonian, we derive an effective input-output relation for a short fiber segment. We then model each fiber segment as a single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel and the entire fiber as a cascade of quantum channels. We then compute the quantum Fisher information for general SBS-dependent parameters and identify optimal measurement settings to achieve the quantum limit, comparing them with receiver-constrained strategies such as heterodyne detection and photon counting. In addition, we propose an adaptive approach that achieves first-order asymptotic optimality and provides a novel second-order correction to address preliminary miscalibration. As an application, we apply the framework to the fiber-tapping detection problem.

motivation: SBS is a powerful mechanism for distributed fiber sensing and intrusion detection, but a quantum treatment of its fundamental limits and optimal measurements was missing.
method: Starting from a linearized opto-acoustic Hamiltonian, the authors derive an effective input-output relation, model each fiber segment as a single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel, compute the quantum Fisher information for general SBS-dependent parameters, and compare receiver-constrained strategies such as heterodyne detection and photon counting, including an adaptive scheme.
result: They identify optimal measurement settings that achieve the quantum limit, propose an adaptive approach with first-order asymptotic optimality and a second-order correction for miscalibration, and apply the framework to fiber-tapping detection.
conclusion: The work provides a quantum information-theoretic foundation for SBS-based fiber sensing, establishing quantum limits and practical measurement strategies for intrusion detection.

title: Optimal Linear-optical Interferometers For Unitary T-designs In A Multi-photon Fock Space
authors: Robert A. Grinshtein, Ivan V. Dyakonov, Stanislav S. Straupe
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the construction of unitary [MATH]-designs in a multi-photon Fock space on programmable linear-optical interferometers. Using the frame potential as the optimization objective, we identify architectures that realize approximate unitary 1- and 2-designs with considerably fewer controllable parameters than required for universal linear optics. title: Second Quantization And Compactness Of Induced Gaussian Quantum Markov Semigroups
authors: Zheng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterize compactness of the Hilbert-Schmidt semigroups induced by finite-mode Gaussian quantum Markov semigroups with a faithful normal invariant state. A unitary second-quantization representation for every [MATH]-embedding shows that compactness at one positive time, compact resolvent, drift stability, and uniqueness of the normal invariant state are equivalent. Examples show that compactness does not require the existence of a spectral gap and that a spectral gap need not imply compactness when the invariant state is not unique.

authors: J. Christiansen-Salameh, D. J. Temples, R. Linehan, S. Sussman, Aloyse Maille, F. Abouzahr, L. Alexis, K. Anyang, D. Bowring, G. Bratrud, E. Celi, A. H. Col\'on Cesan\'i, R. Khatiwada, D. abstract: ArXiv:2610.12556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The integration of low-loss dielectrics into superconducting circuits is of importance to the functionality of quantum computers and sensors. title: A Robust Digital Receiver Architecture For Continuous-variable Quantum Key Distribution
authors: Lu Fan, Xuesong Xu, Miao Yu, Zhengyu Li, Yunsong Yin, Hao Shi, Xuanyu Guo, Song Yu, Yichen Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution utilizes advanced digital signal processing techniques to mitigate channel impairments, driving the progress of high-performance quantum secure communications. Specifically, digital heterodyne receivers are commonly implemented using down-conversion algorithms to detect both components simultaneously where the signal is modulated onto an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and bypass stringent optical phase-locking requirements. However, a rigorous analysis of the quantum security implications of the digital down-conversion algorithm remains absent. In this paper, we investigate the algorithm process from the perspective of quantum operator evolution, revealing that the frequency folding effect inherent in down-conversion inevitably mixes the image-frequency information into the baseband signal. To address this issue, we propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme based on dual-path digital heterodyne receiver. By performing a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain, this scheme perfectly cancels out the image-frequency operator physically. The robust receiver architecture preserves the baseband noise-suppression advantages, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric optical detection losses, and fundamentally closes the image-frequency crosstalk. Practical experiments have validated the feasibility of the proposed architecture and its effective suppression of image-frequency noise, achieving a performance of 11.4 Mbps @ 42 km. This work lays a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for future high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

motivation: Digital down-conversion in CV-QKD heterodyne receivers causes frequency folding that mixes image-frequency information into the baseband, yet the quantum security implications remain unanalyzed.
method: Analyzes the down-conversion algorithm through quantum operator evolution, then proposes a non-equal weighted combination of output operators from two optical paths to physically cancel the image-frequency operator.
result: The architecture suppresses image-frequency noise, achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric detection losses, and experimentally reaches 11.4 Mbps over 42 km.
conclusion: Provides a theoretical and algorithmic foundation for high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

title: Dissipative Majorana Chain---Anomalies And Non-Invertible Symmetries
authors: Tokiro Numasawa Hung-Hsuan Teh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study symmetries and anomalies of dissipative Majorana chains described by Lindblad dynamics. Using the operator-state mapping, we represent the Lindbladian as a non-Hermitian operator on a doubled Hilbert space. In this formulation, the ket and bra contours admit strong fermion parities and strong translations, while their diagonal combinations define weak symmetries. For even and odd chain lengths, we diagnose anomalies by comparing symmetry algebras with and without weak fermion-parity defects. These algebras retain the lattice precursor of the modulo-[MATH] anomaly of the closed Majorana chain and exhibit projective relations between strong fermion parity and weak translation, as well as between weak fermion parity and strong translation, which are intrinsic to open quantum systems. We establish the IR correspondence between the lattice symmetry algebras and those of the doubled Majorana CFT in four spin sectors, identifying chiral fermion parities emanated from the lattice translations. Finally, we develop the lattice bosonization of the dissipative chain. For even length with collective energy dephasing, combining the defect and no-defect sectors and imposing GSO projections gives rise to an Ising Lindbladian with non-invertible Kramers--Wannier symmetries descending from the anomalous strong translation and fermion parity of the Majorana chain. For odd length, constructing mutually commuting ket- and bra-sector spin operators instead yields an Ising Lindbladian with a Kramers--Wannier duality defect. Our results provide a controlled framework for extending lattice anomalies and non-invertible symmetries to open quantum systems.

title: Latent Symmetry In Quantum Zeno Dynamics
authors: Stefano Longhi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Zeno dynamics constrains a continuously monitored system to measurement-selected subspaces. Here we show that the structure of such Zeno subspaces can be governed by a , namely a symmetry that is absent from the geometry of the underlying physical network. We consider a minimal circuit-QED network of coupled microwave resonators subject to quantum-nondemolition (QND) monitoring of local photon occupations. Two distinguished resonators are geometrically inequivalent, yet are exactly exchanged by a latent symmetry of the network. Strong monitoring partitions the single-excitation Hilbert space into three quantum-Zeno subspaces, two of which correspond to localization on the distinguished resonators. Latent symmetry exactly exchanges these two Zeno subspaces and enforces identical escape and residence statistics despite their different microscopic environments. In the strong-measurement regime their residence times grow linearly with the measurement strength and diverge in the ideal Zeno limit, where the measurement subspaces become dynamically disconnected. Our results show that latent symmetry can act as a hidden organizing principle of quantum Zeno dynamics, imposing exact relations between measurement-selected subspaces that are geometrically inequivalent in the physical system.

motivation: Quantum Zeno dynamics confines continuously monitored systems to measurement-selected subspaces, but the structural principles that organize these Zeno subspaces are not well understood.
method: A minimal circuit-QED network of coupled microwave resonators is subjected to QND monitoring of local photon occupations; a 'latent symmetry' absent from the physical geometry is shown to exchange two distinguished resonators and their associated single-excitation Zeno subspaces.
result: Strong monitoring partitions the single-excitation Hilbert space into three Zeno subspaces, and latent symmetry enforces identical escape and residence statistics for the two inequivalent resonators; residence times grow linearly with measurement strength and diverge in the ideal Zeno limit.
conclusion: Latent symmetry acts as a hidden organizing principle of quantum Zeno dynamics, imposing exact relations between measurement-selected subspaces that are geometrically inequivalent in the underlying physical network.

It connects to fundamental questions about how measurement alters dynamics (quantum Zeno effect) and how symmetries—especially hidden ones—can dictate observable phenomena. The use of latent symmetry, a concept from graph theory, introduces an interdisciplinary angle that could inspire new research in quantum control and network science. For a researcher interested in quantum physics, this paper offers insights into measurement-induced localization, subspace engineering, and the role of symmetries beyond geometric ones, with potential applications in quantum simulation and information processing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a novel and elegant theoretical study that uncovers a hidden organizing principle—latent symmetry—in quantum Zeno dynamics. The combination of a minimal, experimentally relevant model with exact analytical results makes it a significant contribution to the understanding of measurement-induced phenomena. The findings are likely to stimulate further theoretical and experimental work on symmetry-protected Zeno subspaces and their applications in quantum technologies. While the study is limited to a small network and ideal conditions, its conceptual novelty and clarity outweigh these limitations. Overall, it is a high-quality paper suitable for a specialized journal like Advanced Quantum Technologies, offering a fresh perspective on the interplay between symmetry, measurement, and dynamics.

title: A Catalytic Algorithm For Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries With Tight Query Bounds
authors: Yu-Ao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary [MATH] using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements [MATH] transpositions or inversions with [MATH] or [MATH] total queries, respectively. More generally, we prove that exact transposition and inversion of an unknown [MATH], [MATH], require at least [MATH] and [MATH] processing queries, respectively, in fixed causal order. These processing bounds hold for any program state prepared independently of the input state using finitely many forward queries, even if that state is consumed during processing. Both our catalytic qutrit algorithms attain their respective bounds. Moreover, exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries requires at least three preparation queries, and our construction attains this bound.
tldr: The paper constructs catalytic algorithms for transposing and inverting unknown qutrit unitaries using forward queries, with tight query bounds.
motivation: Efficient manipulation of unknown quantum operations using only forward queries is a fundamental task, but exact transposition and inversion with minimal queries remain challenging.
method: The work designs deterministic circuits that prepare a catalyst with three queries, then use four processing queries for transposition and eight for inversion, and proves lower bounds for any fixed-causal-order protocol.
result: Exact qutrit transposition requires at least four processing queries and three preparation queries, and the construction attains these bounds; inversion uses eight processing queries and also meets its bound.
conclusion: The catalytic approach achieves optimal query complexity for transposing and inverting unknown qutrit unitaries, providing a tight characterization of the necessary resources.

title: When Irrelevance Governs: Dissipation-regression Scaling In Open Quantum Criticality
authors: Fan Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The real-time dynamics of quantum phase transitions in open systems coupled to finite-temperature environments sits at the heart of contemporary condensed-matter and quantum-information science. Here, invoking a Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, we uncover that, within the coherence-dominated regime of critical real-time evolution, a dissipative coupling deemed naively irrelevant determines, counterintuitively, the longest timescale that holds sway. Possessing a well-defined temporal scaling dimension, it engenders a novel dissipation-regression scaling that systematically reproduces the unusual Kibble-Zurek scaling and relaxation observed in recent numerical studies. By contrast, dissipation-dominated dynamics behaves qualitatively differently. There, furthermore, we show that the discretized and diagonalized formulations of the same open quantum Ising chain realize distinct universality classes.
tldr: The paper studies real-time critical dynamics in open quantum systems and finds that a naively irrelevant dissipative coupling governs the longest timescale via a new dissipation-regression scaling.
motivation: Quantum phase transitions in open systems coupled to finite-temperature environments are central to condensed-matter and quantum-information science, but the role of seemingly irrelevant dissipation in critical real-time dynamics remains unclear.
method: Using a Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, the authors analyze coherence-dominated critical evolution and compare it with dissipation-dominated dynamics for open quantum Ising chains in discretized and diagonalized formulations.
result: An irrelevant dissipative coupling acquires a well-defined temporal scaling dimension and yields dissipation-regression scaling that reproduces unusual Kibble-Zurek scaling and relaxation seen in numerics; dissipation-dominated dynamics behaves qualitatively differently, and the two formulations realize distinct universality classes.
conclusion: Irrelevant dissipative couplings can control long-time critical dynamics, providing a framework for open quantum criticality and highlighting formulation-dependent universality classes.

title: Warm-Start Quantum Computation For Energy Readout And State Preparation
authors: Tien D. Kieu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating a ground-state energy and preparing a ground state both split into a front-end that supplies an approximate state [MATH] and a back-end that reads or refines it. We argue, and measure at every step, that the only thing crossing that split is the front-end's spectral weight distribution [MATH] over the eigenstates of the problem Hamiltonian [MATH]. Everything downstream is priced in it, so the front-end is a swappable module, and we swap it seven times without altering anything to its right. We call the arrangement WARP. Four back-ends spend that distribution. A readout (A) samples [MATH] on the device and extracts true eigenvalues by classical signal processing, returning an energy below the variational bound of the state it was handed, from a signal [MATH] shorter than a Fourier transform needs. Three routes spend the same account on a state instead. An adiabatic schedule (B) has a minimum gap set by the overlap; a discrete amplification (C) is cheaper in depth but must halt at an index the overlap fixes, so it needs a measured value and not a bound; a recursion (D) of depth [MATH] raises the question of whether it can be run at all. The interactions are the substance. On stretched N[MATH] a sample-based diagonalisation reports a variational bound 79 mHa high, fifty times outside chemical accuracy; reading the state it has already prepared returns [MATH] to [MATH] Ha, three orders of magnitude inside it, and needs no new front-end and no new circuit. And because the weights price everything, they must be measurable when scarce, so we beat a weak reference against a strong one and recover overlaps four orders of magnitude below the shot-noise floor. We map the operating envelope throughout, and state the limitations.
tldr: The paper introduces WARP, a modular warm-start framework in which an approximate-state front-end supplies only the spectral weight distribution over the problem Hamiltonian's eigenstates, enabling downstream energy readout and state preparation.
motivation: Ground-state energy estimation and state preparation often depend on approximate input states, but it is unclear what minimal information from the state-preparation stage is actually needed by readout or refinement back-ends.
method: The authors argue that only the spectral weight distribution crosses the front-end/back-end split and test seven interchangeable front-ends with four back-ends, including a sample-based readout, an adiabatic schedule, a discrete amplification, and a recursion.
result: On stretched N2, sample-based diagonalisation yields a variational bound 79 mHa too high, while reading the already-prepared state returns an energy three orders of magnitude inside chemical accuracy; overlap detection also reaches four orders of magnitude below the shot-noise floor.
conclusion: The work establishes a minimal interface for warm-start quantum algorithms, showing that spectral weight information alone can support accurate energy readout and state preparation across interchangeable front-end and back-end modules.

title: Error Mitigation By Zero-Noise Extrapolation (zne) In Indirect-Control System
authors: Masaki Owari Arijit Das
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The indirect-control paradigm offers a scalable approach to quantum computation by restricting external operations to a small subset of qubits, whereas the entire system evolves under its intrinsic many-body Hamiltonian. This framework reduces hardware complexity and limits the noise introduced through control channels. Recently, Anan et al. proposed an implementation of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) within this indirect-control architecture. However, the impact and integration of quantum error mitigation techniques in such a setting remain largely unexplored. In particular, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), a widely used error mitigation strategy, has not yet been systematically adapted to indirect-control VQE. A key requirement of ZNE is the controlled amplification of noise, which is commonly achieved through circuit-level techniques such as unitary folding. In the indirect-control framework, however, quantum operations are largely governed by continuous time-evolution under the system Hamiltonian, making the construction of physically realizable inverse operations non-trivial. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of implementing ZNE within the indirect-controlVQEframework.We address the challenges associated with unitary folding in the presence of time-evolution operators and, with a minimal relaxation of the indirect-control constraint, we propose a ZNE-based error-mitigation strategy that exploits the symmetry of the one-dimensional XY spin chain.
tldr: This paper investigates the feasibility of zero-noise extrapolation error mitigation for variational quantum eigensolver in an indirect-control architecture, proposing a symmetry-based strategy for the 1D XY spin chain.
motivation: Indirect-control quantum computation promises scalable hardware with reduced control noise, but error mitigation techniques like ZNE have not been adapted to its continuous time-evolution dynamics.
method: The authors analyze the obstacles to unitary folding under Hamiltonian evolution and, with a minimal relaxation of the indirect-control constraint, design a ZNE scheme that exploits the symmetry of the one-dimensional XY spin chain.
result: They propose a physically realizable ZNE-based error mitigation strategy for indirect-control VQE, though the abstract does not quantify its performance.
conclusion: The work takes a first step toward integrating error mitigation into indirect-control quantum algorithms and highlights symmetry as a resource for noise amplification.

title: Beyond Hypercontractivity: Stronger Communication Converses Via R\'enyi Contraction
authors: Amedeo Roberto Esposito Ryo Hommura Moore
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the relationship between strong data-processing inequalities for R\'enyi divergences and hypercontractivity. For R\'enyi divergences of order greater than one, we characterize the contraction of R\'enyi divergences through a property of the dual Markov operator that we name power contraction. Using the contraction coefficient, we derive an upper bound on rectangle probabilities in terms of their marginals that is at least as strong as the corresponding bound obtained via hypercontractivity. Combining this result with inversion of the binary R\'enyi divergence, we derive communication lower bounds for one-way communication-assisted agreement distillation. Examples involving binary symmetric and rare-event Z-channels illustrate the improvements over standard hypercontractive converses.
tldr: The paper characterizes contraction of Rényi divergences via a power-contraction property of dual Markov operators and derives communication lower bounds for agreement distillation that are stronger than hypercontractivity-based converses.
motivation: Strong data-processing inequalities and hypercontractivity are standard tools for proving converse bounds in information theory, but sharper bounds may be obtained through Rényi divergence contraction.
method: The authors introduce power contraction for dual Markov operators, use the contraction coefficient to bound rectangle probabilities in terms of marginals, and invert the binary Rényi divergence to obtain one-way communication-assisted agreement distillation lower bounds.
result: The new bound on rectangle probabilities is at least as strong as the hypercontractive bound, and the resulting communication lower bounds improve upon standard hypercontractive converses for binary symmetric and rare-event Z-channels.
conclusion: Rényi contraction provides a general framework for stronger communication converses beyond hypercontractivity, with applications to agreement distillation.

title: Analog Quantum Simulation Of Shastry-Sutherland Ising Materials
authors: Vahagn Mkhitaryan, Milan Kornja\v{c}a, Mao Lin, Alexander Schuckert, Majd Hamdan, Sergio H. Cant\'u, Ammar Ali, Tommaso Macr\'i, Nathan Gemelke, Alexander Keesling, Peter Komar, Travis S. Humble, Alexei Bylinski, Pedro L. S. Lopes, Fangli Liu, Alexandra Boltasseva, Mikhail D. Lukin, Arnab Banerjee, Vladimir M. Shalaev, Sheng-Tao Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frustrated magnets host rich emergent behavior because competing interactions generate dense manifolds of low-energy states. The Ising Shastry-Sutherland model is a paradigmatic setting, motivated experimentally by Ising-like rare-earth tetraborides such as TmB[MATH] and ErB[MATH], whose field-induced magnetization plateaus have motivated extensive microscopic modeling. Yet how tunable quantum fluctuations reorganize this material-motivated phase diagram remains largely unexplored. Here, we realize a transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice using a programmable Rydberg-atom array. We map its quantum phase diagram using density matrix renormalization group calculations and probe corresponding signatures experimentally in arrays containing more than 110 atoms. Beyond the established classical phases, the calculations identify two regimes absent in the classical limit and stabilized at finite transverse field: a [MATH] filling plateau whose finite stability region emerges from a classically degenerate phase boundary and a symmetry-preserving quantum-dimer regime replacing classically selected collinear order. Experiments on finite open arrays reveal signatures consistent with these regimes across three boundary-pinning conditions, with the resulting response maps agreeing qualitatively with the calculated phase diagram. Our results establish programmable Rydberg-atom arrays as tools for exploring frustrated, material-motivated Hamiltonians and motivate searches for new, quantum-driven magnetization plateaus and quantum-dimer behavior in ErB[MATH] under a transverse field or in strain-tuned TmB[MATH].
tldr: A programmable Rydberg-atom array realizes the transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, revealing quantum-driven phases beyond the classical limit.
motivation: Frustrated magnets such as rare-earth tetraborides exhibit rich field-induced magnetization plateaus, but how tunable quantum fluctuations reorganize the material-motivated phase diagram remains largely unexplored.
method: The authors simulate the Ising Shastry-Sutherland model using a Rydberg-atom array with over 110 atoms, compute the quantum phase diagram via density matrix renormalization group (DMRG), and experimentally probe signatures under three boundary-pinning conditions.
result: Calculations identify two regimes absent in the classical limit at finite transverse field: a 1/2-filling plateau and a symmetry-preserving quantum-dimer regime replacing collinear order, with experimental response maps qualitatively agreeing with the calculated phase diagram.
conclusion: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays are established as tools for exploring frustrated material-motivated Hamiltonians, motivating searches for quantum-driven magnetization plateaus and quantum-dimer behavior in ErB4 and strain-tuned TmB4.

title: Continuous-wave Ac Magnetometry Up To Hundreds Of Megahertz Using Nitrogen-vacancy Centers Under A Strong Transverse Magnetic Field
authors: Ryusei Okaniwa, Rui Suzuki, Yuichiro Matsuzaki, Norio Tokuda, Junko Ishi-Hayase
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are promising quantum sensors for AC magnetic fields. However, conventional dynamical-decoupling-based magnetometry becomes technically demanding at high frequencies because of the requirement for increasingly short and high-power microwave pulses. This paper describes an AC magnetometry technique based on continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR) measurements, which enables the detection of signals in the hundred-MHz range. By applying a strong static magnetic field transverse to the NV axis, the energy separation between the relevant electron-spin states was tuned and resonantly coupled with the target radiofrequency (RF) magnetic field, thereby forming RF-dressed states. Unlike pulsed dynamical-decoupling schemes, this approach does not require high-power microwave pulse sequences. The key feature of our method is that the detectable frequency can be tuned by controlling the bias magnetic field strength. Using this methodology, we have experimentally achieved the frequency-tunable detection of AC magnetic fields from 14.4-632 MHz. The sensitivity was 0.558 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 14.4 MHz and 24.4 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 632 MHz. We characterized the field-dependent ODMR contrast and linewidth, and found that their degradation at large transverse fields is a important factor limiting the high-frequency sensitivity. These results establish a simple CW-ODMR approach for widely tunable RF magnetic-field sensing without high-power pulsed spin control.
tldr: A continuous-wave ODMR technique using a strong transverse magnetic field enables tunable AC magnetometry with NV centers up to 632 MHz without high-power microwave pulses.
motivation: Conventional dynamical-decoupling-based AC magnetometry becomes technically demanding at high frequencies because it requires increasingly short and high-power microwave pulse sequences.
method: A strong static magnetic field transverse to the NV axis tunes the electron-spin energy separation into resonance with a target radiofrequency field, forming RF-dressed states that are detected via continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR).
result: Frequency-tunable detection of AC magnetic fields from 14.4 to 632 MHz was achieved, with sensitivities of 0.558 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 14.4 MHz and 24.4 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 632 MHz; degradation of ODMR contrast and linewidth at large transverse fields limits high-frequency sensitivity.
conclusion: This CW-ODMR approach provides a simple, widely tunable RF magnetic-field sensing method without requiring high-power pulsed spin control.

title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms For Bounded-Error Lwe With Few Samples
authors: Prashant Nalini Vasudevan Haoxing Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size [MATH] over prime moduli [MATH], for any fixed [MATH], with errors bounded by [MATH], in time [MATH] given [MATH] original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by [MATH], the same time bound holds with errors bounded by [MATH] and only [MATH] samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples [MATH] [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the [MATH] problem, with a suitable norm bound [MATH] and [MATH] variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.
tldr: The paper gives a subexponential-time algorithm for bounded-error LWE using few samples, improving the sample complexity of the Kirchner-Fouque BKW-style attack.
motivation: LWE is a core hard problem in post-quantum cryptography, and understanding its solvability with limited samples and bounded errors is crucial for assessing cryptographic security.
method: The authors analyze a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style LWE algorithm using elementary bounds on the lower moments of a Fourier statistic, instead of a lattice-chain interpretation.
result: They show that decision and search LWE with bounded secret and error can be solved in subexponential time using only a small number of samples, improving prior sample requirements.
conclusion: This provides a simpler proof and tighter sample complexity for subexponential LWE algorithms, with implications for lattice-based post-quantum cryptography.

title: Gaussian Broja Partial Information Decomposition In Closed Form
authors: Ohad Sheelo, Tal Golan, Ari Pakman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The BROJA partial information decomposition provides an operationally motivated way to separate the information that two sources carry about a target into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. For continuous and high-dimensional variables, however, computing the BROJA decomposition requires solving a difficult optimization problem. Previous work showed that, when each source-target pair is jointly Gaussian, the problem can be reduced to finite-dimensional numerical optimization. Here, we derive a closed-form solution to this optimization problem, enabling direct computation of the BROJA decomposition in the general multivariate Gaussian setting. The resulting closed-form expression enables speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude for high-dimensional Gaussian BROJA PID. Code is available at [URL].
tldr: The paper derives a closed-form solution for the BROJA partial information decomposition in the multivariate Gaussian setting, enabling fast computation of unique, redundant, and synergistic information components.
motivation: Computing the BROJA partial information decomposition for continuous and high-dimensional variables is challenging due to a difficult optimization problem, even for jointly Gaussian source-target pairs where prior work only reduced it to finite-dimensional numerical optimization.
method: The authors analyze the optimization problem for Gaussian BROJA PID and derive an exact closed-form expression for the decomposition components, eliminating the need for numerical optimization.
result: The closed-form expression yields speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude for high-dimensional Gaussian BROJA PID compared to previous numerical methods.
conclusion: This work provides an efficient and exact tool for computing partial information decomposition in Gaussian systems, with potential applications in fields that analyze multivariate dependencies.

title: Improved Classical Optimization Of Fermionic Hamiltonians Beyond Gaussian States
authors: Ojas Parekh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm that approximates the largest eigenvalue [MATH] of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian [MATH] on [MATH] modes. The algorithm achieves energy at least [MATH] and outputs either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis. This is achieved through a new upper bound on [MATH] in terms of the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and [MATH].
tldr: A polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm approximates the largest eigenvalue of traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonians using Gaussian or sparse Fock states.
motivation: Optimizing fermionic Hamiltonians is central to quantum many-body physics and complexity, but classical approaches are often limited to Gaussian states.
method: The paper derives a new upper bound on the largest eigenvalue in terms of the maximum Gaussian-state energy and an additional term, then uses it to construct a randomized classical algorithm.
result: The algorithm outputs a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse Fock-basis state with an energy guarantee, improving on prior Gaussian-state-only bounds.
conclusion: This work extends classical optimization of fermionic Hamiltonians beyond Gaussian states, with implications for approximating ground-state energies.

title: Trainable Quantum-Native Language Models: Dissipative Memory, Capacity Limits, And Hardware Validation
authors: Deniz Yunus G\"o\u{g}\"u\c{s}
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study byte-level autoregressive language models whose hidden state is a small quantum register, whose transitions are learned token-conditioned quantum channels, and whose next-byte probabilities come directly from Born-rule measurements without a learned classical vocabulary projection or softmax. In the fixed-width recurrent setting, unitary dynamics cannot contract or reset stored distinctions; experimentally, unitary recurrence loses to its retrained one-token control in every tested variant. Introducing learned dissipation, then token-conditioned dissipative gating, yields useful memory beyond one token. The gated model improves test negative log-likelihood by 0.20 +/- 0.03 nats/byte over retrained parameter-matched one-token controls at context length 12, and by 0.29-0.33 at longer contexts, but never beats retrained two-token controls. A key-value recall benchmark shows a width-dependent threshold: one stored pair meets the pre-registered accuracy bar at 4-5 memory qubits, two pairs at 6-7, and three pairs remain unsolved. This is consistent with, but does not establish, a capacity explanation for the short effective memory horizon. As a secondary result, one-qubit models reach lower stationary memory entropy than a heuristically optimized classical predictive frontier at matched error in 9/9 seeds. On IBM Heron hardware, computational-basis memory-register distributions show signal against a uniform null in 12/12 circuits across prefixes of up to 12 tokens, next-bit probabilities pass pre-registered accuracy bars at four-token prefixes, and bytes are generated autoregressively by sampling physically measured bit probabilities. The tested models are classically simulable and substantially worse than classical n-gram baselines. We claim no computational quantum advantage.
tldr: A study of byte-level autoregressive language models with a small quantum register as hidden state, showing that learned dissipation enables limited memory but no advantage over classical baselines.
motivation: To explore quantum-native language models and whether dissipative quantum dynamics can provide useful memory beyond simple unitary recurrence.
method: Train token-conditioned quantum channels on a quantum register with Born-rule measurements, compare unitary versus dissipative gating, benchmark key-value recall, and validate on IBM Heron hardware.
result: Dissipative gating improves test negative log-likelihood over one-token controls by 0.20–0.33 nats/byte but never beats two-token controls; recall capacity scales with qubit number, with three pairs unsolved; hardware shows signal but models remain classically simulable and worse than n-gram baselines.
conclusion: Dissipative quantum memory offers limited benefits and no quantum advantage; capacity limits constrain effective memory horizon, and the tested models are not competitive with classical baselines.

title: Post-Quantum Session Establishment For Matter Over Thread: Message Size, Transport, And Protocol Options
authors: Daniel Commey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.
tldr: Quantifies the cost of migrating Matter's CASE handshake to post-quantum cryptography over Thread, showing that drop-in ML-KEM/ML-DSA exceeds message limits and degrades multi-hop performance, and proposes hybrid and cached-chain mitigations.
motivation: Matter's operational handshake, CASE, still relies on P-256 ECDH, leaving recorded traffic vulnerable to harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks once quantum computers exist.
method: A byte-exact model of CASE messages and a Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter constants, evaluate FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms under fragmented IPv6 datagram transport and retransmission timers.
result: A drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB, and no fully post-quantum FIPS 203/204/205 configuration fits Matter's 1178-byte message limit; multi-hop delays increase 1.8–2.6× versus selective-repeat transfer, with up to 33% handshake failures for sleepy devices.
