method: The authors define Safety Graph over a shared propositional state space, give a sound and complete compilation to a classical AI planning problem, and perform A*-based plan search to discover cross-layer cascade paths, validated via Web3D simulation of the Tennessee Eastman chemical plant benchmark.
result: The planning compilation automatically discovers safety-response-induced lateral movements and identifies unaccounted-for barriers, with a complexity and scalability analysis characterizing behavior as model size and cascade depth grow.
conclusion: SG is claimed to be the first framework to formally model bidirectional IT-OT cascade attacks and to let operators explore cyber attacks that trigger cascading safety failures in ICS.

title: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities In Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
authors: Yuying Wang (institute Of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, China, University Of Chinese Academy Of Sciences, China), Yi Guo (institute Of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, China), Jiachi Chen (the State Key Laboratory Of Blockchain,data Security, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou High-Tech Zone), Hanwen Zhang (institute Of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy Of Sciences, China, University Of Chinese Academy Of Sciences, China), Yi Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. Current tools provide limited documented coverage of CVV patterns, while only two of four evaluated LLMs outperform an all-pattern constant baseline of 29.3% Macro-F1; the best reaches 51.2%. Together, the limited tool coverage and inconsistent LLM gains motivate detection methods tailored to cross-chain verification semantics.
tldr: This paper presents the first systematic empirical study of cross-chain verification vulnerabilities (CVVs) in blockchain bridge smart contracts, deriving 11 patterns from 588 audit reports and building a dataset of 830 instances.
motivation: Cross-chain bridges rely on smart contracts with complex verification logic for external-chain data, and incorrectly implemented logic leads to severe security vulnerabilities that are not well characterized.
method: The authors manually analyze 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects to derive 11 CVV patterns grouped into 5 categories, then construct a labeled dataset mapping reports, code versions, affected files, and patterns; they evaluate existing detection tools and four LLMs against an all-pattern baseline.
result: Existing tools have limited documented coverage of CVV patterns, and only two of four LLMs outperform a constant baseline of 29.3% Macro-F1, with the best reaching 51.2%.
conclusion: The limited tool coverage and inconsistent LLM performance motivate the development of detection methods tailored to cross-chain verification semantics.

title: Polyconvex Neural-network Surrogates With Learned Paired Directional Features For Anisotropic Hyperelastic Homogenization
authors: S. Ares de Parga, A. Cornejo, J. A. Hern\'andez, R. Rossi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Approximating the effective anisotropic hyperelastic response of a representative volume element (RVE) requires constitutive expressiveness, mechanical consistency, and computational efficiency. This work develops a polyconvex physics-augmented neural network (PANN) construction based on paired directional features whose orientations, stretch powers, and determinant exponents adapt to the RVE response. The features are composed with convex, componentwise nondecreasing cores, realized as an input-convex neural network (ICNN) or an input-convex Kolmogorov-Arnold network (ICKAN). The complete energies satisfy objectivity, an exactly stress-free reference, two-dimensional polyconvexity, and prescribed growth conditions by construction, and nonnegative energy is certified separately for the selected models. On a multicavity and a single-cavity periodic cell, these energies are compared with an Unconstrained energy, trained identically without the curvature and growth constraints, and with three hyperreduced projection-based reduced-order models (HPROMs), which serve as physics-based references. On the first cell, learning the features lowers the stress error sevenfold, and six features suffice on both. The constrained energies remain below one percent in stress error and in the displacement error of a tensile-coupon FE[MATH] application with a full-order reference, whereas the Unconstrained energy and the HPROMs are more accurate inside the data. Beyond the data, however, the Unconstrained energy loses rank-one convexity, and under confined compression it stops below half of the 500 MPa that the constrained energies reach. These results quantify what the guarantees cost in accuracy and what they secure beyond the data.
tldr: The paper develops polyconvex physics-augmented neural network surrogates with learned paired directional features for approximating the effective anisotropic hyperelastic response of representative volume elements.
motivation: Homogenizing anisotropic hyperelastic materials requires surrogate models that are simultaneously expressive, mechanically consistent (polyconvex, objective), and computationally efficient.
method: Paired directional features with adaptable orientations, stretch powers, and determinant exponents are composed with convex nondecreasing cores (ICNN or ICKAN), guaranteeing objectivity, stress-free reference states, 2D polyconvexity, and growth conditions by construction.
result: Learning the features reduces stress error sevenfold, with constrained energies staying below one percent stress and displacement error; unlike the unconstrained baseline and HPROMs, they retain rank-one convexity and reach 500 MPa under confined compression.
conclusion: The construction quantifies the accuracy cost of enforcing convexity and consistency guarantees while securing robust behavior outside the training data.

title: Limit Theorems For Random Matrix Products With A Simple Top Lyapunov Exponent
authors: Dominique Malicet Pablo G. Barrientos
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study products of independent, identically distributed random matrices with an exponential moment and a simple top Lyapunov exponent, without assuming irreducibility. Outside an exceptional invariant subspace called the equator, we establish contraction on average for a weighted projective distance and a spectral gap for the associated Markov operator. We obtain a central limit theorem, a Berry--Esseen bound, deviation estimates near the mean, and an almost sure invariance principle both for the growth of a fixed vector outside the equator and for the operator norm. For fixed vectors, a non-arithmeticity assumption also yields a local limit theorem and a renewal theorem. Our contraction criterion applies more generally to mostly contracting random maps on locally compact spaces with a Lyapunov function, including certain random interval maps.
tldr: The paper proves limit theorems for products of i.i.d. random matrices under a simple top Lyapunov exponent without irreducibility, including central limit theorems, Berry-Esseen bounds, deviation and renewal results.
motivation: Random matrix products are central in dynamical systems, probability, and statistical physics, but many limit theorems require irreducibility or other restrictive assumptions. The authors aim to extend such results under weaker hypotheses.
method: They introduce contraction on average for a weighted projective distance outside an exceptional invariant subspace called the equator, establish a spectral gap for the associated Markov operator, and derive probabilistic limit theorems.
result: They obtain a central limit theorem, Berry-Esseen bound, deviation estimates, almost sure invariance principle, and, under non-arithmeticity, a local limit theorem and renewal theorem for fixed vectors and operator norms.
conclusion: The contraction criterion applies more generally to mostly contracting random maps on locally compact spaces with a Lyapunov function, including certain random interval maps.

title: Sddp Has Polynomial Iteration Complexity In The Horizon
authors: Vincent Leclere
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) and its variants are run in practice with forward passes that sample the noise at random. Recent iteration-complexity results favour another choice: when the trial points are selected deterministically, for instance along the scenario with the largest gap, the number of iterations is polynomial in the horizon [MATH], whereas every bound we know of for randomly sampled forward passes is exponential in [MATH]. We show that this is not intrinsic to random sampling, for a broad class of trajectory-following dynamic programming algorithms, which includes SDDP, stochastic dual dynamic integer programming and stochastic Lipschitz dynamic programming. With random sampling, and with Lipschitz constants, diameters and per-stage loss ranges bounded independently of the stage and of the horizon, the expected number of iterations whose policy is not [MATH]-optimal is [MATH], where [MATH] is the state dimension: linear in [MATH], as for deterministic selection rules. The proof needs no particular scenario to be sampled: the gap between the expected cost of the current policy and the current lower bound equals the expected sum of one-step Bellman residuals along the sampled path, and Lipschitz cuts that are tight at the visited states turn the positive residuals into permanent increases of a bounded potential. The results extend to noise without finite support, to backward passes on a sample average approximation, and to stationary and periodic infinite-horizon SDDP with geometric pass lengths.
tldr: The paper proves that stochastic dual dynamic programming with random forward sampling has polynomial iteration complexity in the horizon under bounded Lipschitz constants, diameters, and per-stage loss ranges.
motivation: SDDP and related trajectory-following dynamic programming methods are widely used with random forward passes, but existing complexity bounds for random sampling were exponential in the horizon, unlike deterministic selection rules.
method: The authors analyze a broad class of trajectory-following dynamic programming algorithms, including SDDP, stochastic dual dynamic integer programming, and stochastic Lipschitz dynamic programming, using a potential-function argument based on expected Bellman residuals and Lipschitz cuts.
result: They show that the expected number of iterations with a non-epsilon-optimal policy is linear in the horizon, matching deterministic selection bounds, and extend the results to noise without finite support, sample average approximation backward passes, and infinite-horizon SDDP.
conclusion: Random sampling is not inherently worse than deterministic sampling for the iteration complexity of this algorithmic class, provided the relevant Lipschitz and range parameters are uniformly bounded.

title: Detecting Random Geometric Graphs With General Kernel
authors: Shuangping Li Dong Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study testing a random geometric graph with a fixed kernel against an Erds-R\'enyi graph with the same edge density. Under the null hypothesis, the graph has [MATH] vertices and independent edges with probability [MATH]. Under the alternative hypothesis, latent points [MATH] are independent and uniform on [MATH], and edges are conditionally independent with probabilities [MATH], where [MATH]. The goal is to determine a critical dimension [MATH]: the total variation distance between the two graph laws tends to one for [MATH] and to zero for [MATH]. For dense graphs, [BDER16] established [MATH] for hard threshold kernels, whereas [MWX26] proved [MATH] for smooth kernels with [MATH]. We connect these results by characterizing the detection thresholds for kernels that need not be differentiable at zero. We also determine the thresholds for smooth kernels whose first nonzero derivative at zero has finite order greater than one. Throughout these classes, signed triangle or quadrilateral counts attain the optimal detection threshold. For certain nondifferentiable kernels, quadrilateral counts are optimal while triangle counts are suboptimal.
tldr: This paper characterizes detection thresholds for distinguishing random geometric graphs with general kernels from Erdős–Rényi graphs of the same edge density.
motivation: Previous work established thresholds only for hard threshold kernels and smooth kernels, leaving a gap for general kernels that may be nondifferentiable or have higher-order derivatives at zero.
method: The authors analyze the total variation distance between the two graph laws and use signed triangle and quadrilateral counts to derive optimal detection thresholds.
result: The critical dimension depends on the kernel's behavior at zero; signed triangle or quadrilateral counts attain optimal thresholds, with quadrilateral counts being optimal for certain nondifferentiable kernels.
conclusion: The work provides a unified characterization of detection thresholds across kernel classes, connecting and extending prior results on random geometric graph detection.

title: Low-Complexity SVD-Based Precoding Over Zero-Padded Isi Channels
authors: Amin Sakzad Shuiyin Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a low-complexity SVD-based transceiver for zero-padded memory-[MATH] ISI channels. Appending a single zero-padding symbol to an [MATH]-symbol block yields an [MATH] channel matrix with an . This structure provides closed-form singular values and vectors, enabling exact SVD precoding and equalization via FFTs without explicitly forming dense SVD matrices. The resulting implementation has [MATH] complexity and incurs only a [MATH] rate penalty. The resulting parallel scalar subchannels enable joint adaptive PAM and power allocation for SER minimization, followed by exact soft-information computation for LDPC decoding. At comparable code rates near [MATH], simulations show that our proposed scheme outperforms a conventional TX-FFE/RX-DFE system with hard-decision Reed-Solomon (RS) decoding by approximately [MATH] dB at FER [MATH]. At high SNR, it achieves nearly the same FER performance as a SOVA-based receiver with LDPC decoding, while replacing trellis-based detection with fast SVD precoding and exact scalar soft-output computation.
tldr: A low-complexity SVD-based precoding and equalization scheme for zero-padded ISI channels that exploits the channel matrix structure to enable FFT-based implementation and improved coded performance.
motivation: Conventional equalization for intersymbol interference channels can be computationally complex, and efficient precoding methods are needed for high-rate communication with low implementation cost.
method: Appending a zero-padding symbol to an M-symbol block yields a structured channel matrix with closed-form singular values and vectors, allowing exact SVD precoding and equalization via FFTs without forming dense matrices.
result: The proposed scheme achieves O(M log M) complexity with a small rate penalty; simulations show about 1 dB improvement over TX-FFE/RX-DFE with hard-decision RS at a given FER and near-SOVA LDPC performance at high SNR.
conclusion: The structured SVD approach provides an efficient alternative to trellis-based detection, enabling adaptive PAM and power allocation with exact soft information for LDPC decoding.

title: A Kernel-independent precorrected-FFT Method
authors: Owen Melia Tristan Goodwill
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The precorrected-FFT has been used to rapidly evaluate [MATH]-body sums arising in electromagnetics and acoustics settings. It has, however, been historically limited to kernels that satisfy a Green's identity. In this work, we demonstrate that, using an improved version of the method of proxy points, the precorrected-FFT can be used to efficiently compute [MATH]-body sums with a wide variety of kernels. This algorithm requires no analytic information beyond pointwise access to the kernel. Our examples include kernels from non-local PDEs, Matern kernels, anisotropic kernels, and the Green's functions of high order PDEs. We also provide a detailed algorithm for choosing the proxy points and spreading grid, as implemented in the new pcfft package. We show these algorithmic choices result in favorable scaling when compared to other kernel-independent fast summation methods. Finally, we use the algorithm to accelerate a wide variety of integral equations solvers involving non-standard kernels, with applications in surface scattering, geophysics, and microbial community formation.
tldr: The paper presents a kernel-independent precorrected-FFT method for fast N-body summation using proxy points and no analytic kernel information beyond pointwise access.
motivation: The precorrected-FFT was historically restricted to kernels satisfying a Green's identity, limiting its applicability to general kernels.
method: The authors improve the method of proxy points and provide a detailed algorithm for choosing proxy points and the spreading grid, implemented in the pcfft package.
result: The approach efficiently computes N-body sums for a wide variety of kernels, including non-local PDE kernels, Matérn kernels, anisotropic kernels, and high-order PDE Green's functions, with favorable scaling compared to other kernel-independent fast summation methods.
conclusion: The method accelerates integral equation solvers for non-standard kernels, with applications in surface scattering, geophysics, and microbial community formation.

title: Numerical Smoothness And Error Analysis For Evolution Equations
authors: Tong Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This is a lecture note to introduce the innovative concept of numerical smoothness and its application in the error analysis of numerical solutions of evolution equations. We start from the two fundamentally different error splittings. One splitting is popular, which brings us to local error defined along the original solution and error propagation by numerical schemes. The well know Lax Equivalence Theorem is based on this error splitting. The other splitting can only be seen in a few numerical ODE books, which brings us to local error defined along the numerical solution and error propagation by the solutions of the evolution equations. The innovative concept of numerical smoothness arises from the second error splitting. While there are many difficulties when we use numerical stability in error analysis of nonlinear evolution equations, we will show that numerical smoothness works naturally in error analysis/estimation/control with advantages in several ways. We will define temporal and spatial numerical smoothness indicators, prove the necessity of the boundedness of these indicators for having optimal convergence rate, and show computable error estimates as functions of these smoothness indicators. Moreover, these error estimates are optimal in the approximatons' convergence rates and also optimal in the error propagation of the evolution equation. In comparison with error analysis framework of the Lax Equivalence Theorem, from the necessity results and the error estimates proven in the numerical smoothness framework, we have a new equivalence theory: Consistency + Numerical Smoothness <=> optimal error estimates. Unlike the Lax Equivalence Theorem, the new equivalence theory works well for nonlinear problems, nonlinear schemes, and many other complications of problems.
tldr: This lecture note introduces numerical smoothness as a new framework for error analysis of numerical solutions to evolution equations.
motivation: Error analysis for nonlinear evolution equations is challenging when using traditional numerical stability concepts, motivating an alternative framework based on a different error splitting.
method: The paper defines temporal and spatial numerical smoothness indicators, proves their boundedness is necessary for optimal convergence, and derives computable error estimates in terms of these indicators.
result: It establishes a new equivalence theory—Consistency + Numerical Smoothness <=> optimal error estimates—that works for nonlinear problems and schemes where the Lax Equivalence Theorem struggles.
conclusion: Numerical smoothness offers advantages over classical stability-based error analysis and extends error estimation/control to nonlinear settings.

title: Khintchine Dichotomy For Images Of Self-similar Measures And Almost Random Walks
authors: Liyang Shao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Following the celebrated breakthrough in B\'enard-He-Zhang, we prove Khintchine dichotomy for push-forwards of self-similar measures on [MATH] under uniform [MATH] maps. For this, we also study almost random walks on [MATH] and prove their effective equidistribution.
tldr: The paper proves a Khintchine dichotomy for push-forwards of self-similar measures under uniform maps and establishes effective equidistribution for almost random walks.
motivation: The work follows a breakthrough by Bénard-He-Zhang and aims to extend Khintchine-type dichotomy results to images of self-similar measures.
method: The author studies almost random walks on a group and proves their effective equidistribution, then applies this to push-forwards of self-similar measures.
result: A Khintchine dichotomy is established for the images of self-similar measures under uniform maps, along with effective equidistribution for almost random walks.
conclusion: The results contribute to fractal geometry and homogeneous dynamics, but have no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Representing The Non-dominated Set Of Multi-objective Optimization Problems With Polyhedral Ordering Cones
authors: Michael Stiglmayr Chiara Weuste
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the literature, research on representing the non-dominated set has focused almost exclusively on multi-objective optimization problems with Pareto-dominance. However, general ordering cones are used to incorporate preferences of decision makers into the optimization process and to model other specific types of optimization problems, such as ordinal optimization problems. In this work, we consider several representation approaches based on representation relations in the context of multi-objective optimization problems with polyhedral ordering cones. Our main research question is whether existing theory and solution approaches developed for the Pareto case can be used to address the more general setting.
tldr: This paper studies representation approaches for the non-dominated set of multi-objective optimization problems defined by polyhedral ordering cones, generalizing beyond Pareto dominance.
motivation: Preferences and specialized optimization problems often require ordering cones broader than Pareto dominance, but representation theory has focused almost exclusively on the Pareto case.
method: The authors formulate representation relations for multi-objective optimization with polyhedral ordering cones and investigate whether existing Pareto-based theory and solution methods extend to this general setting.
result: They analyze several representation approaches and clarify which results from Pareto-dominance multi-objective optimization carry over to polyhedral ordering cones and which require adaptation.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for representing non-dominated sets under general polyhedral preference cones, extending classical multi-objective optimization concepts beyond the Pareto framework.

title: Hausdorff Dimension And Flexibility For Attractors Of Non-Uniformly Hyperbolic Flows
authors: Paulo Varandas Elias Rego
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Hausdorff dimension of attracting sets of three-dimensional flows whose one-dimensional quotient dynamics is non-uniformly expanding. Our main assumption is that the quotient map admits a full-branch uniformly expanding Gibbs--Markov induced map. We first prove that every such attractor contains a hyperbolic horseshoe of Hausdorff dimension strictly larger than two. As a consequence, after an arbitrarily small [MATH] perturbation, the associated dynamical Lagrange and Markov spectra have robustly non-empty interior for an open and dense set of [MATH]-observables. We then establish intermediate dimension properties. Every admissible intermediate Hausdorff dimension is realized by an ergodic invariant measure supported on the attractor. Moreover, every intermediate stable and unstable dimension is realized by a strictly ergodic hyperbolic subsystem. The approach extends the dimension theory previously developed for geometric Lorenz attractors to more general non-uniformly hyperbolic attractors including singular-hyperbolic attractors, Rovella attractors, and broad classes of skew-product suspension flows modeled by intermittent and Benedicks--Carleson maps.
tldr: The paper studies the Hausdorff dimension and flexibility of attractors for three-dimensional non-uniformly hyperbolic flows, including results on hyperbolic horseshoes and Lagrange/Markov spectra.
motivation: The authors aim to extend dimension theory from geometric Lorenz attractors to broader classes of non-uniformly hyperbolic attractors, such as singular-hyperbolic and Rovella attractors.
method: They assume a full-branch uniformly expanding Gibbs-Markov induced map for the one-dimensional quotient dynamics and use this to prove dimension results via ergodic theory and perturbation arguments.
result: They show that every such attractor contains a hyperbolic horseshoe of Hausdorff dimension strictly larger than two, and that every admissible intermediate Hausdorff or stable/unstable dimension is realized by ergodic invariant measures or strictly ergodic hyperbolic subsystems.
conclusion: The work generalizes the dimension theory of geometric Lorenz attractors and establishes robust non-empty interiors for dynamical Lagrange and Markov spectra under small perturbations.

title: Numerical Stability Of Extended-Domain Spectral Collocation: Floating-Point Regularization And An Equilibrium Law For The Frame Constants
authors: Po-Yi Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended-domain spectral collocation expands the solution of a boundary value problem in the Laplacian eigenbasis of an enclosing box and collocates at as many nodes as modes. The square system is exponentially ill-conditioned, and the impossibility theorem for equispaced data rules out stable geometric convergence; yet such solvers converge geometrically to a few orders of magnitude above the unit roundoff. We explain why in one dimension. The collocation solution is the solution operator applied to the interpolant of the data in an operator-dependent test space whose Lebesgue constant must grow exponentially for geometric convergence, so exact solutions can amplify data errors exponentially. In floating-point arithmetic the error of any coefficient vector is bounded by its nodal residual, its distance to a competitor and two frame constants, a leakage and a restricted Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund constant, bounded uniformly in the number of modes at a fixed positive threshold; for a backward-stable solve, under a condition on the perturbed matrix, the bound is uniform in the conditioning for suitably analytic data and, with computed constants, within a factor of about ten of the error floor of a direct solver. For the Poisson operator the rate of the two constants along the tail of the spectrum is given by a constrained equilibrium problem of logarithmic potential theory. For an interval of length [MATH] extended by [MATH] at each end, the problems for [MATH] and [MATH] are dual, the rate is linear for [MATH], and it starts with slope minus the fraction of the extended domain occupied by the extension, so for [MATH] the leakage constant obeys no power law with the exponent of the end of the spectrum. In experiments, convection--diffusion operators behave like the Poisson operator at moderate P\'eclet numbers.
tldr: The paper analyzes the floating-point numerical stability of extended-domain spectral collocation and derives an equilibrium law governing the frame constants that control error growth.
motivation: Extended-domain spectral collocation produces exponentially ill-conditioned square systems, yet such solvers often converge geometrically to a few orders above unit roundoff; the paper seeks to explain this behavior in one dimension.
method: The collocation solution is expressed as a solution operator applied to a data interpolant in an operator-dependent test space; error bounds involve nodal residual, distance to a competitor, and two frame constants (leakage and restricted Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund), whose tail rate is characterized by a constrained equilibrium problem of logarithmic potential theory.
result: At a fixed positive threshold the frame constants are bounded uniformly in the number of modes; for backward-stable solves with suitably analytic data the bound can be uniform in conditioning and within about a factor of ten of a direct solver's error floor, and for the Poisson operator the constant rate is linear and depends on the fraction of the extended domain occupied by the extension.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical explanation for the observed stability of extended-domain spectral collocation and establishes an equilibrium law for the frame constants, with experiments showing convection-diffusion operators behave similarly at moderate Péclet numbers.

title: Banach Space, Birkhoff--James Orthogonality, James Constant, Von Neumann--Jordan Constant
authors: Qi Liu Zhiyao Fang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a strengthened answer to the questions posed by Alonso, Mart\'in, and Papini [Studia Math. 188 (2008), 135--150] concerning the comparison between the von Neumann--Jordan and James constants . The classical inequality [MATH] between the von Neumann--Jordan and James constants was established by Takahashi and Kato [J. Math. Anal. Appl. 359 (2009), 602--609], Wang [Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 138 (2010), 695--701], and Yang and Li [Appl. Math. Lett. 23 (2010), 277--281], while related sharp estimates were obtained by Kato and Takahashi [Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo (2) Suppl. 82 (2010), 75--91]. We sharpen this inequality to [MATH], where [MATH] is the Birkhoff--James orthogonal James constant introduced by Baronti and Papini [Constr. Math. Anal. 5 (2022), 37--45]. Our proof employs optimal distance ellipses and alternating contact directions.
tldr: The paper sharpens a known inequality comparing the von Neumann--Jordan constant and the James constant in Banach spaces using the Birkhoff--James orthogonal James constant.
motivation: It addresses questions of Alonso, Martín, and Papini on comparing geometric constants of Banach spaces and improving prior inequalities by Takahashi, Kato, Wang, and Yang--Li.
method: The proof uses optimal distance ellipses and alternating contact directions to strengthen the inequality involving the Birkhoff--James orthogonal James constant.
result: The classical inequality between the von Neumann--Jordan and James constants is improved by incorporating the Birkhoff--James orthogonal James constant.
conclusion: This work advances the geometric theory of Banach spaces and refines the relationship between fundamental constants, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Finite-Sample Bounds For Fr\'echet Means Of Dependent Data In Metric Spaces With Curvature Bounded Above
authors: Christof Sch\"otz Zoraida F. Rico
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove finite-sample risk bounds for empirical quadratic and power Fr\'echet means in geodesic metric spaces with curvature bounded above for observations with arbitrary joint law. We compare the sample with exchangeable copies in which one observation is redrawn independently of the original sample and the others move to preserve the joint law. These displacements control the error, with no entropy or dimension assumptions. For quadratic Fr\'echet means, this yields a general ``coupling bound'' in any separable complete [MATH] space, where for [MATH] the observations must lie in a closed convex set of circumradius below [MATH]. This bound is exact on the real line for nonnegatively correlated Gaussian observations and for comonotone functions of a common factor. We apply it in two settings. Under local dependence, the resulting risk bound grows linearly with the average size of the dependency neighborhoods. Under transport sensitivity and for bounded metric variances, summable sensitivities of the conditional laws to a change in one observation preserve the parametric mean squared error rate, while nonsummable polynomial decay gives explicit slower rates. We verify transport sensitivity for stationary reversible Markov chains with Wasserstein-contractive kernels and for bi-Lipschitz images of Gaussian sequences. In the more challenging setting of heavy-tailed, dependent data with possibly infinite variance, we consider power Fr\'echet means of order [MATH]. Under nonpositive curvature, we bound their [MATH] risk assuming only finite [MATH]-th moments.
tldr: The paper derives finite-sample risk bounds for empirical quadratic and power Fréchet means in geodesic metric spaces with curvature bounded above, for arbitrarily dependent observations.
motivation: Classical empirical-process bounds for Fréchet means typically assume independence or entropy/dimension conditions; the authors aim to obtain risk bounds that hold for data with arbitrary joint law and no entropy or dimension assumptions.
method: By comparing the sample with exchangeable copies in which one observation is redrawn and the others are displaced so as to preserve the joint law, the authors derive a general coupling bound, then specialize it to local dependence, transport sensitivity, and heavy-tailed dependent data with power Fréchet means of order p.
result: The coupling bound is exact on the real line for nonnegatively correlated Gaussians and comonotone functions of a common factor; under local dependence the risk grows linearly in the average neighborhood size, summable transport sensitivities preserve the parametric MSE rate, and under nonpositive curvature the L^p risk of power Fréchet means is bounded given only finite p-th moments.
conclusion: The framework supplies dimension-free, entropy-free finite-sample guarantees for Fréchet means of dependent data in nonpositively/upper-curvature-bounded metric spaces, extending parametric-rate behavior to a range of dependence structures.

title: SoK: Privacy-Preserving Order Matching
authors: Prerna Arote, Adrian Saiz, Lucianna Kiffer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy-preserving order matching enables traders to discover and execute compatible orders while limiting disclosure of sensitive trading information. Existing systems span financial markets and blockchain-based asset exchanges and employ diverse market structures, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions, making their privacy guarantees difficult to compare. We present a systematization of privacy-preserving order matching covering 22 protocol families. We organize the order lifecycle into four phases: order representation and submission, order discovery and collection, order-matching, and settlement, and characterize each phase by protected and exposed information, access roles, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions. Our analysis shows that privacy is not a single protocol-level property: protecting selected order attributes or individual phases does not necessarily prevent leakage elsewhere in the lifecycle. We identify recurring trade-offs among privacy, functionality, trust, and verifiability, highlighting the challenge of achieving end-to-end privacy across the complete order lifecycle.
tldr: This systematization of knowledge reviews 22 protocol families for privacy-preserving order matching and analyzes privacy leakage across the order lifecycle.
motivation: Existing privacy-preserving order matching systems span financial markets and blockchain-based exchanges with diverse market structures, mechanisms, and trust assumptions, making their privacy guarantees difficult to compare.
method: The authors organize the order lifecycle into four phases—order representation/submission, discovery/collection, order-matching, and settlement—and characterize each phase by protected and exposed information, access roles, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions.
result: The analysis shows privacy is not a single protocol-level property: protecting selected attributes or individual phases does not necessarily prevent leakage elsewhere, revealing recurring trade-offs among privacy, functionality, trust, and verifiability.
conclusion: Achieving end-to-end privacy across the complete order lifecycle remains a key challenge, and the paper provides a comparative framework for evaluating and designing future systems.

title: Enabling Extended Sgx Enclaves Inside Confidential Virtual Machines
authors: Pamenas Kariuki, Dong Yiliang, Quoc Do Le, Christof Fetzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS). This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~[MATH]s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.
tldr: TEEVisor introduces an AMD SEV-SNP-based architecture for nesting Intel SGX-compatible and extended eSGX process enclaves inside confidential virtual machines.
motivation: Confidential VMs and process enclaves offer complementary security properties, and nesting enclaves within CVMs could address long-standing SGX limitations in isolation, transition cost, and programming flexibility.
method: The paper designs TEEVisor, a CVM-resident security monitor and kernel driver that uses AMD SEV-SNP VMPLs to create hardware-protected process-level enclaves with SGX binary compatibility and an extended eSGX mode.
result: On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, about 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to 93 [MATH]s/MB.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use, improving enclave programming and performance while preserving hardware-based protection.

title: Better Batches, Better Privacy: Random Allocation For DP-BandMF
authors: Arun Ganesh Ryan Mckenna
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The current state of the art for batch selection and noise addition in differentially private training is a combination of DP-BandMF (informally, DP-SGD where the noise added in two different steps can be correlated if the steps are within [MATH] of each other) and privacy amplification by sampling via Monte Carlo accounting. First, whereas prior batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF were inspired by Poisson sampling, random allocation is known to outperform Poisson sampling for DP-SGD. We therefore propose and analyze new batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF inspired by random allocation, improving RMSE by up to [MATH] over previous work. Second, Monte Carlo accounting typically requires drawing [MATH] samples from a privacy loss distribution, making accounting costly. We increase sampling and scoring throughput by two orders of magnitude through a carefully optimized GPU implementation. Finally, previous work chose the DP-BandMF strategy matrix and the batch selection strategy independently. We give a simple framework for choosing these parameters jointly, reducing RMSE by up to [MATH] over fixed strategy matrices.
tldr: The paper improves batch selection and parameter tuning for DP-BandMF in differentially private training, with GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo accounting.
motivation: Differentially private training methods such as DP-SGD and DP-BandMF benefit from better batch selection and noise correlation strategies to reduce error, but existing batch selection and accounting methods leave room for improvement.
method: The authors propose random-allocation-inspired batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF, develop a highly optimized GPU implementation of Monte Carlo privacy accounting, and introduce a framework for jointly choosing the strategy matrix and batch selection parameters.
result: Their strategies improve RMSE by up to a stated factor over prior work, they achieve two orders of magnitude higher accounting throughput, and joint parameter selection reduces RMSE by up to another factor.
conclusion: The work advances practical differentially private machine learning by providing better batch allocation, faster accounting, and joint optimization of privacy parameters.

title: Onions In The ATmosphere: Decentralizing Trust In Identity
authors: Nick Gerakines Paul Syverson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiple approaches have been implemented for identities that associate meaningful identifiers, such as domain names, with self-authenticating identifiers, such as onion addresses. While these approaches offer various advantages both from identifier meaningfulness and from identifier self-authentication, identifier association itself is subject to blocking, hijack, fingerprinting, and other forms of surveillance and manipulation. So too are the resources associated with an identity comprising a meaningful identifier and a self-authenticating identifier. This paper describes ongoing work on two such approaches to self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI): associating a registered domain name with an onion address (onion association) and associating an atproto handle with a decentralized identifier (DID association). We present both the application of already implemented and published means of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in a single identity. Finally, we describe grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust, wherein trusting attestations of identity relies on contextual relevance of an attestor to the identity rather than relying only on structural authority, for example as embodied in the traditional centralized infrastructure.
tldr: This paper describes ongoing work on self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI) by combining onion address association with DID association and grounding trust in contextual attestations rather than centralized authority.
motivation: Existing approaches to associating meaningful identifiers like domain names with self-authenticating identifiers like onion addresses are vulnerable to blocking, hijacking, fingerprinting, and surveillance, as are the resources linked to such identities.
method: The authors apply already implemented and published secure onion association methods to DID association and combine both into a single identity, then propose grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust based on attestor relevance.
result: The paper presents the application of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in one identity, along with a contextual trust framework for attestations.
conclusion: Decentralizing trust in identity can be advanced by integrating self-authenticating meaningful identifiers and relying on contextual relevance of attestors instead of traditional centralized infrastructure.

title: Network Topology Shapes Ai Intervention Effectiveness On Deception: Truth-Telling Vs. Investigative Agents
authors: Zhao Song, Stefan Sarkadi, The Anh Han
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deploying AI agents to combat dishonest communication is an intuitive response to deception in hybrid human-AI societies. However, the efficacy of such interventions in realistic networked settings remains unclear. We study this problem using an evolutionary game-theoretic model of the Deceiver's Game by extending it to structured networks, where agents can adopt deception, truth-telling, and investigation strategies. We introduce committed AI agents (zealots) fixed to either truth-telling or investigative strategies and conduct agent-based simulations across three network topologies. Our key findings are: (1) passive committed truth-telling agents can amplify adaptive deception by creating exploitable honest partners, whereas investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in the oscillatory regime; (2) intervention effects are non-monotonic in deployment density because committed agents reshape rather than simply suppress the underlying oscillatory dynamics; and (3) response peaks depend on topology, with sampled scale-free populations showing sharp low-density responses and fully connected populations requiring larger committed fractions. Overall, the results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed agents to influence networked deception dynamics.
tldr: This paper uses evolutionary game theory on structured networks to study how committed AI agents with truth-telling or investigative strategies affect deception dynamics.
motivation: The authors aim to understand whether deploying AI agents to combat deceptive communication in hybrid human-AI societies works in realistic networked settings, since intuitive interventions may backfire or have topology-dependent effects.
method: They extend the Deceiver's Game to structured networks with agents choosing between deception, truth-telling, and investigation, introduce committed AI zealots, and run agent-based simulations on three network topologies.
result: Passive truth-telling zealots can amplify adaptive deception, while investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in oscillatory regimes; effects are non-monotonic in deployment density and depend on network topology.
conclusion: The results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed AI agents to influence networked deception dynamics.

title: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization For Permissionless Ai Markets
authors: Jianting Zhang, Zhongtang Luo, Aniket Kate
abstract: ArXiv:2610.12948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads. Experimental results show that under attacks with up to 10,000 synthetic Sybil identities and with chosen attackers, the payment exposure and capacity depletion remain bounded. Regarding practicality, the witness-commit mechanism lowers admission cost by up to 40.8% compared with baselines, and admitting common payments costs approximately \[MATH]0.21.
tldr: AgentValve is a blockchain-based protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI service markets, using a trust network with finite-capacity reputation and smart-contract-enforced capacity reservation.
motivation: Permissionless AI markets allow adversaries to cheaply create many identities and fabricate feedback, inflating provider reputation and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss through Sybil attacks on reputation-based payment authorization.
method: The protocol models reputation as finite capacity in a directed trust graph and authorizes payments via trust paths with available capacity, using smart contracts to atomically reserve capacity and a witness-commit mechanism for efficient off-chain route discovery and on-chain verification.
result: Experiments using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads show bounded payment exposure and capacity depletion under attacks with up to 10,000 Sybil identities, with up to 40.8% lower admission cost than baselines.
conclusion: AgentValve provides a practical Sybil-resilient payment authorization layer for permissionless AI markets, bounding honest agents' exposure and reducing verification overhead through cryptographic commitments.

title: Space Over Statistic, Retraining Over Ranking: Auditing Training Labels Under Label-Only Backdoors
authors: Mohammad Mahfuzul Islam Arnab Dey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some backdoor attacks never touch an image. FLIP only changes labels: on CIFAR-10, flipping 3% of them makes a ResNet-32 send 99.7% of triggered source-class images to the attacker's class. The usual defenses look for the poison inside a model trained on those same labels. So when they struggle, is the problem the test they run, or the space they run it in? We answer with a controlled swap: we keep the test, the labels and the metric fixed, change only the feature space, and judge each defense by retraining the victim on what it keeps. The space decides. On dog[MATH]cat the same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on the poisoned model's features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features that never saw a label, and 0.995 on the same network trained on clean labels, an oracle control rather than a defense. We reproduce SPECTRE, the defense FLIP's authors recommend, to 90.94 / 0.97 against its published 91.47 / 1.7, then price it: on truck[MATH]deer it deletes 20% of every class, while a prototype audit on the frozen features deletes 6% for higher clean accuracy and lower attack success. On three harder pairs that audit leaves about a quarter of the attack standing. A count read off encoder geometry and clean labels, before any attack is run, separates the pair where the audit removes the attack from those where it only partly does, though on a single zero-count pair. Three results warn against the easy story. A better detection score does not mean a safer model: on two of four pairs Confident Learning scores the higher AUROC, and on dog[MATH]cat leaves 2.6 times the attack success. The prototype family, our best static performer, is the first an adaptive attacker slips past. And past a point, catching more poisons stops reducing attack success. Check labels in a space that never learned them, and judge a defense by the retrained model, not by its detection score.
tldr: The paper audits label-only backdoor defenses by swapping feature spaces while holding labels, tests, and metrics fixed, and shows that defense performance depends more on the feature space and should be judged by retrained victim models rather than detection AUROC alone.
motivation: Label-only backdoor attacks such as FLIP evade image-based poison detection, and existing defenses are evaluated in the poisoned model's feature space, making it unclear whether failures stem from the detection method or the representation space used.
method: The authors perform a controlled feature-space swap on CIFAR-10 pairs, fixing labels and metrics, and evaluate defenses by retraining the victim on retained samples; they also reproduce SPECTRE and compare prototype audits on frozen DINOv2 and clean-trained features.
result: Same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on poisoned-model features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features, and 0.995 on clean-label-trained oracle features; SPECTRE deletes 20% of every class on truck–deer, whereas a prototype audit deletes 6% with better clean accuracy and lower attack success.
conclusion: Defense evaluations should use feature spaces that never learned the labels and should be judged by retrained-model attack success rather than detection scores, because higher AUROC does not guarantee a safer model and adaptive attackers can bypass top static detectors.

title: Cape - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine For Vulnerability Scoring And Management
authors: Rakesh Podder, Viktoria Koscinski, Indrajit Ray
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows that CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority than all baselines, demonstrating that context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.
tldr: CAPE is a context-aware vulnerability prioritization framework that enriches scanner reports with deployment-specific evidence to rank CVEs for remediation.
motivation: Traditional vulnerability scoring systems like CVSS, EPSS, and KEV are context-free and their differing goals lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions and misallocated remediation efforts.
method: CAPE performs reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis on enriched vulnerability data, producing a ranked priority score; evaluated on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs.
result: Many CVEs are not reachable or exploitable, causing significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines (CVSS, EPSS, KEV); CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority.
conclusion: Context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.

title: The Limits Of Query Monitoring Against Distributed Model Extraction
authors: Snigdha Chandan Khilar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, benign evaluation pipelines look exactly like distillation, we found no deployable detector at colluder shares of 2.5% or below, and campaigns that relay real users' requests may be invisible to any query-only monitor.
tldr: This paper studies the theoretical and empirical limits of query-only monitoring for detecting distributed model extraction campaigns against large language model providers.
motivation: Model providers face distillation campaigns spread across many accounts that individually appear benign, and when metadata cannot link accounts, query patterns are the only evidence available.
method: Using one million real chat turns for development and 17 held-out weeks for evaluation, the authors formalize detection limits and test calibrated spectral and coordination-based monitors against naive and padded distributed extraction campaigns.
result: A calibrated monitor detects naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss in 0.86-1.00 of weeks, and one variant detects topical-text-padded campaigns in 0.50-0.96 of weeks, but slow ramp-up campaigns evade calibration, benign evaluation pipelines resemble distillation, and no deployable detector was found at colluder shares of 2.5% or below.
conclusion: Query-only monitoring has concrete detectability limits rooted in benign coordination, and some distributed extraction campaigns, especially those relaying real users or operating at low colluder shares, may remain invisible.

title: Compact Quantitative Equational Theories As Monad Restrictions
authors: Colin Riba Matteo Mio
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proofs in quantitative algebra are, generally, infinite objects due to the presence of infinitary rules in the deductive apparatus. A quantitative equational theory is called compact if all its consequences are derivable by means of finite proofs, that is, proofs not using any instances of the infinitary rules. This definition is purely logical. In this work we give an equivalent, but categorical, characterisation based on the notion of monad restriction.
tldr: This paper gives a categorical characterization of compact quantitative equational theories via monad restrictions.
motivation: Quantitative equational theories often involve infinitary proofs, and compactness (all consequences derived by finite proofs) is a purely logical property worth characterizing categorically.
method: The authors use category theory, specifically monads and their restrictions, to model quantitative equational theories and their compactness.
result: They show that compactness of a quantitative equational theory is equivalent to a condition on the associated monad restriction.
conclusion: This provides a new categorical perspective on compactness in quantitative algebra, bridging logic and category theory.

title: Understanding And Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks Via Persistent Artifacts In Agent Skill Composition
authors: Dianshu Liao, Shidong Pan, Guangdong Bai, Zhenchang Xing, Xiaoyu Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills extend the capabilities of AI agents by bundling instructions, code, and resources into reusable packages. During skill execution, agents may produce or modify artifacts, such as files, configurations, and cached data, that are reused by other skills in later sessions. Since these artifacts can persist across sessions and later be accessed by other skills, they introduce a new attack surface that can be exploited to influence subsequent executions. However, the security risks arising from such cross-session skill interactions remain largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents and develop a runtime defense against them. Specifically, we characterize three attack mechanisms, namely Instruction Propagation (IP), Data Boundary Violation (DBV), and Evidence Poisoning (EP), through which malicious effects propagate across skill executions via persistent artifacts. To evaluate whether existing agents can resist these attacks while completing legitimate tasks, we construct SkillRelayBench, a benchmark of 270 adversarial cases drawn from 30 cross-session skill-composition scenarios across ten domains. Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%. Successful attack chains cover all five target security consequence categories, highlighting the broad impact of these attacks. To mitigate these risks, we propose SkillRelayGuard, which restores artifact provenance context and provides pre-execution advisory review while leaving the final execution decision to the agent. Evaluation across three agent settings shows that SkillRelayGuard reduces overall ASR from 69.5% to 10.9% and ACSR from 54.8% to 10.0%, while increasing legitimate task completion from 79.6% to 87.5%.
tldr: The paper investigates cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents via persistent artifacts and proposes SkillRelayGuard as a runtime defense.
motivation: Agent skills can produce persistent artifacts that are reused across sessions and skills, creating a new attack surface whose security risks remain largely unexplored.
method: It characterizes Instruction Propagation, Data Boundary Violation, and Evidence Poisoning, builds SkillRelayBench with 270 adversarial cases, evaluates seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code, and proposes SkillRelayGuard to restore artifact provenance and provide pre-execution advisory review.
result: Attack success rates range from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates from 35.6% to 61.1%; SkillRelayGuard reduces ASR from 69.5% to 10.9% and ACSR from 54.8% to 10.0%, while increasing legitimate task completion from 79.6% to 87.5%.
conclusion: Cross-session artifact-based attacks pose a broad threat to agent skill composition, and provenance-aware advisory defense can substantially mitigate them without severely harming legitimate task performance.

title: Quantization-Tolerant Gradient Auditing For Active Inference-Attack Detection In Federated Learning
authors: Michael Kuehne-Schlinkert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. The usual defense, differential privacy, often adds so much noise that the model is no longer worth training. In cross-silo FL, where participants are a few accountable organizations and the server is trusted, we ask whether the server can instead interrogate clients. Each round it sends a secret challenge batch and asks every client to return a checksum of the gradient that batch induces, together with a timing. A client that mutated the model state, as an active generative-adversarial-network discriminator attacker does, returns a wrong checksum. We make this checksum robust to benign cross-platform floating-point non-determinism with a quantized fingerprint compared under a small tolerance. It flags two distinct active attacks at a true-positive rate of [MATH] with no false positives on the checksum axis, stable across the fingerprint's parameters and up to [MATH] clients at malicious ratios to [MATH], for [MATH] of server work and [MATH] per response. Against a purely passive attacker the only signal is timing, and it is not robust: a cohort-relative test detects only in low-jitter conditions while a false-positive-free per-client baseline is blind, so no configuration delivers both. An attacker that answers the challenge on an untouched copy of the model while tampering with a replica evades the audit entirely. Therefore the checksum is a reliable in-band signal against attackers that do not decouple the audited computation from the attacked one, and it composes with differential privacy, whose accuracy cost we quantify on Texas100, rather than replacing it.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantization-tolerant gradient checksum audit for detecting active inference attacks in cross-silo federated learning, showing reliability only against attackers that do not decouple the audited computation from the attacked one.
motivation: Federated learning participants can infer private data from shared models, but differential privacy often adds excessive noise; the trusted server could instead interrogate clients via secret challenge batches.
method: Each round the server sends a secret challenge batch and asks clients for a quantized checksum of the induced gradient plus timing; the checksum is compared under a small tolerance to flag mutated model states, while timing is used for passive attackers.
result: The checksum flags two active attacks with a reported true-positive rate and no false positives on the checksum axis across parameter settings and malicious ratios, but passive attackers are only weakly detectable via timing and decoupled attackers evade the audit entirely; it composes with differential privacy, with accuracy cost quantified on Texas100.
conclusion: The checksum is a reliable in-band signal against coupled active attackers and can complement differential privacy, but it fails when the audited computation is decoupled from the attacked one and is not robust for passive attacks.

title: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents For Reliable Vulnerability Repair
authors: Yilian Shi, Qingyu Liu, Tianyi Zhou, Wende Tan, Chenyang Si, Yueming Lyu, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based approaches for repository-level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent-based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at [URL].
tldr: EviRepair is an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level automated vulnerability repair, using evidence review to improve patch generation and validation.
motivation: Agent-based automated vulnerability repair with LLMs often generates unreliable evidence, undermining vulnerability understanding and patch accuracy.
method: EviRepair enables multiple agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation.
result: Experiments on PatchEval and SecBench show average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates over existing agent-based baselines across multiple frameworks and LLMs.
conclusion: Evidence review significantly improves the reliability and effectiveness of LLM-driven automated vulnerability repair, though the work is outside quantum information research.

title: A Systematic Study Of Security Enforcement At Android Inter-Component Boundaries
authors: Sandiyo Christan A
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Android's inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders, and URI scheme handlers) form the primary interface between applications and between applications and the system. We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary's enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict(), achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data (authentication tokens, payment credentials, medical information) despite the known unverifiability of custom schemes (RFC 8252 Section 8.1). Our study includes 23 positive controls, calibration cases demonstrating that the evaluation procedure distinguishes functioning enforcement from observed enforcement failures.
tldr: A systematic empirical study of Android inter-component boundary security enforcement across 120 evaluations, finding widespread enforcement gaps.
motivation: Android IPC mechanisms are critical attack surfaces, but it is unclear whether platform and application security controls actually function as designed across different interface categories.
method: The paper evaluates 99 inter-component interface cases, 10 platform security-control cases, and 11 positive controls across over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17, using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model.
result: The study finds 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) versus 23 enforcement holds (19.2%), with Activities and BroadcastReceivers showing 100% gap rates, ContentProviders achieving a 27.6% holds rate, and all evaluated platform compatibility changes disabled or gated at unused targetSdkVersion values.
conclusion: The authors derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy and document custom URI schemes handling sensitive data, arguing that Android inter-component security enforcement remains highly inconsistent despite framework-provided defenses.

title: ToFu: Exploiting And Fuzzing The LLM-Orchestrator-Tool Trust Boundary
authors: Md Nazmul Islam Ananto, Pierre Prevost-Avenel, Colin Smith, Kyungtae Kim, Taegyu Kim, Arslan Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that interact with external software through tools, with an orchestration layer translating model outputs into structured tool invocations. This architecture creates an LLM-orchestrator-tool trust boundary where tool semantics may go unenforced and LLM-generated arguments may be incorrectly treated as trusted. We present ToFu, a tool-aware framework that automatically derives semantic security checks for LLM tools from their existing metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus. ToFu specializes these checks to individual tools and automatically generates fuzzing harnesses and semantic oracles using runtime introspection and outcome sanitization. We evaluated ToFu across 273 MCP servers containing 3405 tools and identified verified bugs corresponding to CWE weakness classes in 343 tools across 118 of the servers. Our findings show that real-world tools frequently fail to enforce their documented input semantics, making it unsafe to treat LLM-generated arguments as trusted.
tldr: ToFu automatically derives semantic security checks and fuzzing harnesses for LLM tool integrations, exposing trust-boundary flaws in real-world MCP servers.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly invoke external tools, but the orchestration layer may treat model-generated arguments as trusted and fail to enforce tool semantics.
method: ToFu uses tool metadata and a CWE-guided sanitizer corpus to generate tool-specific semantic checks, fuzzing harnesses, and runtime oracles.
result: Across 273 MCP servers with 3405 tools, ToFu identified verified CWE-related bugs in 343 tools from 118 servers.
conclusion: Real-world LLM tools often do not enforce documented input semantics, making it unsafe to trust LLM-generated arguments without verification.

title: Asymmetric Information In Dynamic Lending Games
authors: Kristijan Atanasov, Frederik Mallmann-Trenn, Carmine Ventre
abstract: ArXiv:2610.13759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a dynamic lending game with limited but reusable supply. Borrower arrivals and loan durations are stochastic. Demand is allocated cheapest-first, subject to available supply, so a lender's quote affects both its current payoff and its ability to serve future borrowers. Motivated by industry practice, we study this problem through the lens of information disclosure: Lenders observe either only their own available supply or also their rivals' aggregate available supply. We ask how providing this information to all, some or none of the lenders affects payoffs as demand varies relative to supply, and how these effects change when a fixed total supply is divided among different numbers of lenders. Interestingly, in the case of asymmetric information disclosure, total payoffs can increase, while total lending remains the same. We identify sufficient mathematical regimes in which this phenomenon occurs. Who receives supply information matters differently as demand rises. For the case of two lenders, informing only the larger lender yields higher total lender payoff at lower demand, while informing only the smaller lender can yield the highest total lender payoff at higher demand. For a platform deciding which lenders can observe rival supply, the results suggest that disclosure can change the fees paid by borrowers without changing how much is lent. Wider access to supply information need not lower those fees: its effect depends on who receives the information and the balance between demand and supply.
tldr: The paper studies how asymmetric information disclosure about rival supply affects payoffs in a dynamic lending game with stochastic borrower arrivals and reusable loan supply.
motivation: Motivated by industry practice, the authors examine whether lenders should observe only their own available supply or also rivals' aggregate supply, and how this affects payoffs as demand varies.
method: They model a dynamic lending game with stochastic arrivals and loan durations, cheapest-first demand allocation, and compare information disclosure regimes using mathematical analysis.
result: They identify regimes where asymmetric information disclosure increases total payoffs without changing total lending, and show that who receives supply information matters differently as demand rises.
